Broadly speaking, I like to differentiate declarative macros based on access level.crate-exported: Intended to be exported from your crate and used by your dependentscrate-local: Intended to be used privately within your crateYou should prefer to keep macros crate-local if possible.Macros can be useful even if you don’t intend on exporting them. Actually, that’s most commonly how I make use of macros!The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

You should prefer to keep macros crate-local if possible.Macros can be useful even if you don’t intend on exporting them. Actually, that’s most commonly how I make use of macros!The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

Macros can be useful even if you don’t intend on exporting them. Actually, that’s most commonly how I make use of macros!The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

For historic reasons, macros have two different ways they scope into the surrounding code.Textual Scoping: The macro scope is based on where in the file it’s definedPath-Based Scoping: The macro becomes an item in the module tree (acting more similarly to a standard Rust item)Where possible, you should prefer path-based scoping, but textual scoping can come in handy in some cases. Additionally, you’re very likely to run into heavy usage of the original textual scoping rules. So it’s worth understanding them regardless.

Where possible, you should prefer path-based scoping, but textual scoping can come in handy in some cases. Additionally, you’re very likely to run into heavy usage of the original textual scoping rules. So it’s worth understanding them regardless.

By default, declarative macros take on a textual scope.Textual scoped declarative macros have some counter-intuitive visibility and access rules.The macro may be used ONLY after its definition within a module, function, or logical scope.The macro may be used by any submodules after the macro definition, even without importing it explicitly.So unlike other parts of the Rust language, order actually matters for textual scoped declarative macros.The most narrow visibility is within a logical scope (for example a function). Sometimes, though admittedly rarely, this can be useful for functions that have a lot of internal repetition.fn example() { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } // You cannot access this macro outside of the function. If the macro is going to be used in multiple items within the same module, you can simply define it in the module itself. This is more visible than within a single function, but it’s still constrained to only the current module and its submodules.// You cannot use it here, because it's not defined yet. macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Now it can be invoked and used. helper_macro!(); // It can be used within functions, as one might expect. fn within_functions() { helper_macro!(); } // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // which might feel counter-intuitive. mod even_within_submodules { helper_macro!(); } Sometimes it can be beneficial to use a macro from the parent module the containing module is defined under.Modern Rust syntax allows for this better with path-based scoping, which we’ll learn about in the next section.That said, you may still run into this syntax, so we should cover it.To hoist macros defined in a submodule into the parent’s textual scope, you can attach the #[macro_use] attribute on the containing module.// We still cannot use `helper_macro!` here, it isn't defined yet. // After the module definition completes, // it's now defined in the parent's textual scope. #[macro_use] mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } // See? Now we can access and use it here even without an import. // It acts as-if we had defined textually after `submodule`. helper_macro!(); // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // since it's a part of the textual scope. mod sibling_submodule { helper_macro!(); } But note that #[macro_use] will not automatically propagate further up the module tree.If you want your macro to continue to be defined all the way up the module tree, you’ll have to continue to attach the #[macro_use] attribute on all the parent modules.#[macro_use] // <- Necessary if you need it... mod outer_file { #[macro_use] mod other_file { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); // <- ... at this location onwards. Historically, #[macro_use] was also used to import external macros from other crates into your textual scope.You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

This is more visible than within a single function, but it’s still constrained to only the current module and its submodules.// You cannot use it here, because it's not defined yet. macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Now it can be invoked and used. helper_macro!(); // It can be used within functions, as one might expect. fn within_functions() { helper_macro!(); } // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // which might feel counter-intuitive. mod even_within_submodules { helper_macro!(); } Sometimes it can be beneficial to use a macro from the parent module the containing module is defined under.Modern Rust syntax allows for this better with path-based scoping, which we’ll learn about in the next section.That said, you may still run into this syntax, so we should cover it.To hoist macros defined in a submodule into the parent’s textual scope, you can attach the #[macro_use] attribute on the containing module.// We still cannot use `helper_macro!` here, it isn't defined yet. // After the module definition completes, // it's now defined in the parent's textual scope. #[macro_use] mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } // See? Now we can access and use it here even without an import. // It acts as-if we had defined textually after `submodule`. helper_macro!(); // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // since it's a part of the textual scope. mod sibling_submodule { helper_macro!(); } But note that #[macro_use] will not automatically propagate further up the module tree.If you want your macro to continue to be defined all the way up the module tree, you’ll have to continue to attach the #[macro_use] attribute on all the parent modules.#[macro_use] // <- Necessary if you need it... mod outer_file { #[macro_use] mod other_file { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); // <- ... at this location onwards. Historically, #[macro_use] was also used to import external macros from other crates into your textual scope.You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

Path-based scoping for declarative macros allows us to work with macros in a way which feels more idiomatic.The macro works a lot like any other item, and can be invoked before the definition.In order to be used, it needs to be manually imported or resolved from the module tree.This can be accomplished with a small bit of code right after the macro definition:macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Re-export as an item in the module tree. pub(crate) use helper_macro; When you do this, since the macro is now a part of the module tree, order no longer matters.// Can call here, even if the macro isn't defined yet. helper_macro!(); macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro; // Can obviously still call here. helper_macro!(); Even though you can refer to macros out of order when they use path-based scoping, you’ll probably still want to define them before they’re used within the same file. Not because it’s necessary, but because it’s readable!The real benefit of this is that other modules can import and use the macro like they would any other item.mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro; } mod another_submodule { // You can use it like a normal item! use crate::submodule::helper_macro; helper_macro!(); // Or you can refer to it by a path! crate::submodule::helper_macro!(); } It’s most common to see this used with pub(crate), but you can really use all item visibilities here (pub(super), pub(in some::path), empty for private). pub has some strange properties, however - we’ll cover that in the next section.

It’s most common to see this used with pub(crate), but you can really use all item visibilities here (pub(super), pub(in some::path), empty for private). pub has some strange properties, however - we’ll cover that in the next section.

If you want a declarative macro to be usable from outside your crate, you have to attach the #[macro_export] attribute to it.Be careful when deciding to export a macro!After you export a macro, users may grow to depend on it, and it may become difficult to change or maintain. This is why I usually err towards not exporting a macro, until I’m sure it’s warranted.Still, if you’re sure it’s the right thing to do, you can accomplish it like so:#[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } mod submodule { use crate::exported_macro; exported_macro!(); } The observable effects of this attribute are:The root of your crate will publicly export the macro for dependents to use (use your_crate::exported_macro).You can privately import the macro using normal path-based scoping (use crate::exported_macro).It doesn’t matter whether the macro is in a submodule or not, it will always export at the root.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { use crate::exported_macro; exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of the `use` statement mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of the `use` statement } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` The #[macro_use] attribute still has an effect privately within your crate, as one would expect for textual scoping rules. Though, I don’t recommend using it on modules containing exported macros, instead just go through the exported path.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { // <- Would not be usable here without a `use` statement #[macro_use] mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_use]` } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` If you want to export a macro somewhere other than the crate root, there’s a way to allow for that.It would be nice if you could just not use #[macro_export], and instead pub use exported_macro, but as for now this doesn’t work. If you try it, you will be met with a compile error that the macro is “only public within the crate, and cannot be re-exported”.So, you MUST use #[macro_export] on exported macros. Then, you can bind that exported macro to a specific location in the module tree with pub use exported_macro.That’s annoying since it’ll publish a macro in the root (which you probably don’t intend), so the general pattern for this is:Hide the publicly exported macro (so folks can’t see it’s actually at the root).Create a public path binding in the module where you want the macro to be accessed from.So, for instance:pub mod submodule { // Since this is `#[macro_export]`, // it will still wind up at the crate root. // // Because of that, we name this in a way that deters usage. // We'll also hide it, so that it doesn't appear in docs. #[doc(hidden)] #[macro_export] macro_rules! __exported_macro { () => {}; } /// The actual documentation will go here! #[doc(inline)] pub use __exported_macro as exported_macro; } // Technically this does export the following macro... crate::__exported_macro!(); // However, documentation will only list this version. // And, this version will be public for dependents to use. crate::submodule::exported_macro!(); In future versions of Rust, this cruft around visibility and module tree exporting may get cleaned up.It’s hard to make changes like this to the Rust language that won’t break existing code. So this has remained one of those weird parts of the language which - if you’re not careful - can work in odd, non-idiomatic ways.There’s a pretty in-depth thread about this here on the Rust internals forum.

Then, you can bind that exported macro to a specific location in the module tree with pub use exported_macro.That’s annoying since it’ll publish a macro in the root (which you probably don’t intend), so the general pattern for this is:Hide the publicly exported macro (so folks can’t see it’s actually at the root).Create a public path binding in the module where you want the macro to be accessed from.So, for instance:pub mod submodule { // Since this is `#[macro_export]`, // it will still wind up at the crate root. // // Because of that, we name this in a way that deters usage. // We'll also hide it, so that it doesn't appear in docs. #[doc(hidden)] #[macro_export] macro_rules! __exported_macro { () => {}; } /// The actual documentation will go here! #[doc(inline)] pub use __exported_macro as exported_macro; } // Technically this does export the following macro... crate::__exported_macro!(); // However, documentation will only list this version. // And, this version will be public for dependents to use. crate::submodule::exported_macro!(); In future versions of Rust, this cruft around visibility and module tree exporting may get cleaned up.It’s hard to make changes like this to the Rust language that won’t break existing code. Recall from our prior article, when we talked about macro hygiene, that Rust uses what’s known as “mixed-site hygiene”.Most items - other than local variables - are resolved from where the macro is invoked (functions, types, traits, etc.). For crate-local macros, you can be a little looser with this and require that the invoking code imports some items as needed to compile. But for crate-exported macros, it’s not a good idea to force the user to do this.Because of that, you should keep the following things in mind:You usually want to avoid using the crate keyword directly, because it may not refer to your crate.Since you’re in less control over the surrounding code for crate-exported macros, you should not assume anything about what has been imported at the invocation site.For declarative macros, there’s a special, always-present meta-variable called $crate, which resolves to the crate that your declarative macro is defined in. So it’s usually prudent to use that as a common reference point for any items needed by your macro’s expansion.// Example type - pretend we have a full type definition. pub struct MyCustomHashMap { /*...*/ } /// A declarative macro that produces a hash map. /// /// Note: Actually, the standard is attempting to add this! /// See: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.hash_map.html #[macro_export] macro_rules! hash_map { ( $( $key:expr => $value:expr ),* $(,)? ) => {{ // Use our hashmap implementation from our crate. let mut map = $crate::MyCustomHashMap::new(); $( map.insert($key, $value); )* map }} } #[test] fn example() { let map = hash_map! { "key" => "value", }; assert_eq!(map.get("key"), Some(&"value")); } In the above example we demonstrate this with a MyCustomHashMap which our crate also exports. Other standing functions, or other required traits, would also need to be resolved via $crate.If your macro depends on items from other crates, it’s often wise to re-export those dependencies in a public module hidden within your crate. We usually name this something like __private and mark it #[doc(hidden)] to deter usage.#[doc(hidden)] pub mod __private { // Publicly re-export things that your macro uses here. } The serde crate does this with its own __private module. Though, their instance of it may be more for their procedural macros (Serialize and Deserialize). After all, this isn’t a problem specific to declarative macros.

Macros very often don’t have a specific type they’re bound to, usually they’re general convenience macros.That being the case, I recommend the following organization strategy:For macros which are constrained to a single module or function, just define them where they’re needed.For macros which are shared across multiple modules, define them in a common parent module.Tip: For smaller crates, this can often be easiest to target the top-most module (lib.rs).I don’t like to carelessly slap macros into some parent module (or I have several of them, which becomes unwieldy). So I put them in separate files for each macro that I define, and then re-export them into some organizational parent module.Crate-exported macros fit into this pretty well. In those cases, I just don’t re-export into the parent if the intended way to access the macro is by from the crate root.This harkens back to my module organization article, where I detail methods of using “organizational modules”, and defining types in their own separate files.Please take a look at that if you are having trouble understanding my organization strategy.mod.rs: (organizational module; often lib.rs)mod macros; mod type_a; mod type_b; mod type_c; // etc... macros/mod.rs: (organizational module)// Modules: mod exported_macro; mod helper_macro_a; mod helper_macro_b; mod helper_macro_c; // etc... // Re-Exports: pub(crate) use helper_macro_a::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_b::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_c::*; // etc... macros/exported_macro.rs:// In this case, I'm happy to bind it to the root. #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } macros/helper_macro_a.rs:macro_rules! helper_macro_a { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro_a; Elsewhere in the crate:// Either pull them in for usage: use crate::macros::{helper_macro_a, helper_macro_b}; helper_macro_a!(); helper_macro_b!(); // Or refer to them via absolute paths: crate::macros::helper_macro_c!(); I know this seems like overkill, but the nice thing about this is I can always very easily find a macro. Either the macro is defined near its usage (so it’s within the same file), or the file is named the same thing as the macro so it’s easy to open via a command.If a macro is very closely related to another macro, and they’re only split up for ease of maintenance, I usually put them in the same file. But I only do that if they are meant to be implementation details of the main macro intended to be invoked.And, you don’t always need an organizing macros module - you could just re-export the macros right into the main organizational module. That’s for each person and project to decide on.

I don’t like to carelessly slap macros into some parent module (or I have several of them, which becomes unwieldy). So I put them in separate files for each macro that I define, and then re-export them into some organizational parent module.Crate-exported macros fit into this pretty well. In those cases, I just don’t re-export into the parent if the intended way to access the macro is by from the crate root.This harkens back to my module organization article, where I detail methods of using “organizational modules”, and defining types in their own separate files.Please take a look at that if you are having trouble understanding my organization strategy.mod.rs: (organizational module; often lib.rs)mod macros; mod type_a; mod type_b; mod type_c; // etc... macros/mod.rs: (organizational module)// Modules: mod exported_macro; mod helper_macro_a; mod helper_macro_b; mod helper_macro_c; // etc... // Re-Exports: pub(crate) use helper_macro_a::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_b::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_c::*; // etc... macros/exported_macro.rs:// In this case, I'm happy to bind it to the root. #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } macros/helper_macro_a.rs:macro_rules! helper_macro_a { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro_a; Elsewhere in the crate:// Either pull them in for usage: use crate::macros::{helper_macro_a, helper_macro_b}; helper_macro_a!(); helper_macro_b!(); // Or refer to them via absolute paths: crate::macros::helper_macro_c!(); I know this seems like overkill, but the nice thing about this is I can always very easily find a macro. Either the macro is defined near its usage (so it’s within the same file), or the file is named the same thing as the macro so it’s easy to open via a command.If a macro is very closely related to another macro, and they’re only split up for ease of maintenance, I usually put them in the same file. But I only do that if they are meant to be implementation details of the main macro intended to be invoked.And, you don’t always need an organizing macros module - you could just re-export the macros right into the main organizational module. That’s for each person and project to decide on.

Now that we know how to integrate declarative macros into our project, let’s look at some use cases for them.At the risk of sounding like a broken record - I would like to remind you to try as hard as possible NOT to export the macro.A crate-local macro, as stated, is really nice because users only depend on the side effects of it. You control the syntax and the places it’s invoked completely. There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

You control the syntax and the places it’s invoked completely. There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

While developing a crate, you may author types that have some nearly-identically-implemented functions or traits.If the types are semantically closely related, we can reduce duplication using a helper macro. The helper macro will implement the common traits or function, with some information provided to it.Some specific examples of when this is beneficial include:If you need to author several types which are mostly simple wrappers of other types (something like a newtype).If you want to ensure several types have an identical subset of an API (functions and traits).Be careful not to reach for declarative macros at the smallest sign of duplication, though. Instead, you should consider it when things appear to be very cut-and-paste. If you over-generalize, that could make maintenance more of a burden, not less.For implementation macros like these, I like to follow a key = value pattern.macro_rules! impl_example { ( input_1 = $input_1:literal, input_2 = ($($input_2:tt)*), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = $grouped_input_1:literal, grouped_input_2 = $grouped_input_2:ident, grouped_input_3 = $grouped_input_3:expr, }, input_4 = [$($input_4:expr),* $(,)?], ) => { /*Expansion Here*/ }; } impl_example! { input_1 = 123, input_2 = (complex; grouped, input), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = "sample", grouped_input_2 = Sample, grouped_input_3 = concat!("..."), // ... }, input_4 = [ array_value_1, array_value_2, array_value_3, // ... ], // ... etc ... } My reason for preferring this syntax is:You cannot accidentally map a fragment to the wrong input without it being visible at the call site.It uses a different binding syntax from struct initialization to distance itself from appearing to initialize an object.Despite the binding syntax being different, it feels familiar enough to be immediately understood.Though, I’ll admit the last two points aren’t that important. If you feel more comfortable you could use a more “struct field initialization” style format (key: value). That’s up to you!Don’t over-generalize these, accept them in one order - we’re only using these internally after all.I sometimes like to order them alphanumerically by key name, so that the order is at least consistent.ExamplesAn example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. Integer types (like u8) use a crate-local int_impl macro to implement common functions and traits.It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. Commonly useful in cases where your trait will just call the same trait on all tuple elements. You can see an example of this in the serde crate with the crate-local tuple_impls! macro.If you’d like a toy example - here’s one using some strongly typed time values. The macro helps us ensure the conversion implementations are consistent between the different types.#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub struct OverflowError; #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Hours(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Minutes(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Seconds(u32); macro_rules! impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

{ from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

Be careful not to reach for declarative macros at the smallest sign of duplication, though. Instead, you should consider it when things appear to be very cut-and-paste. If you over-generalize, that could make maintenance more of a burden, not less.For implementation macros like these, I like to follow a key = value pattern.macro_rules! impl_example { ( input_1 = $input_1:literal, input_2 = ($($input_2:tt)*), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = $grouped_input_1:literal, grouped_input_2 = $grouped_input_2:ident, grouped_input_3 = $grouped_input_3:expr, }, input_4 = [$($input_4:expr),* $(,)?], ) => { /*Expansion Here*/ }; } impl_example! { input_1 = 123, input_2 = (complex; grouped, input), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = "sample", grouped_input_2 = Sample, grouped_input_3 = concat!("..."), // ... }, input_4 = [ array_value_1, array_value_2, array_value_3, // ... ], // ... etc ... } My reason for preferring this syntax is:You cannot accidentally map a fragment to the wrong input without it being visible at the call site.It uses a different binding syntax from struct initialization to distance itself from appearing to initialize an object.Despite the binding syntax being different, it feels familiar enough to be immediately understood.Though, I’ll admit the last two points aren’t that important. If you feel more comfortable you could use a more “struct field initialization” style format (key: value). That’s up to you!Don’t over-generalize these, accept them in one order - we’re only using these internally after all.I sometimes like to order them alphanumerically by key name, so that the order is at least consistent.ExamplesAn example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. Integer types (like u8) use a crate-local int_impl macro to implement common functions and traits.It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. The macro helps us ensure the conversion implementations are consistent between the different types.#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub struct OverflowError; #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Hours(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Minutes(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Seconds(u32); macro_rules! impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. A really popular reason for declarative macros is to match the format! syntax from the standard library.You don’t always need to provide such a macro, sometimes you can just take impl Into and let the user format as they please. But it can make things more readable in cases where the user will always be formatting a string, or if you want formatting to be conditionally compiled-out when disabling alloc support.ExamplesTo point at the standard library again, we can look at the todo! macro. It’s simple enough that it’s just implemented right there as a declarative macro instead of being a built-in like many other macros (similar to assert_eq!, matches!, and a few others).It’s a bit of a low-hanging fruit, but the log crate has some pretty obvious examples; info!, warn!, and error!. In general, anything with a format!-like operation benefits from a declarative macro.assert!-like macros are another example of this kind of macro. You may not think too much about it, but it can be nice to provide added details about a failure for unit tests. The assert! macros all accept format arguments at the end, and you can too if you need some adapter assert! macro.macro_rules! assert_in_range { ($input:expr, $low:expr, $high:expr, $($msg:tt)*) => {{ let input = $input; let low = $low; let high = $high; assert!( input >= $low, "{}: range check failed: {input} >= {low}", format_args!($($msg)*), ); assert!( input <= $high, "{}: range check failed: {input} <= {high}", format_args!($($msg)*), ); }}; } #[test] fn example() { let number = 5; assert_in_range!(number, 50, 100, "formatted example (input={})", number); } The failure here looks like this:thread 'example' (50) panicked at src/lib.rs:22:5: formatted example (input=5): range check failed: 5 >= 50 note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

For many types, you can get away with either the struct initialization format, or using the builder pattern.#[derive(Default)] struct Example { foo: u8, bar: String, baz: bool, } // Some initialization patterns: fn struct_initialization() { let object = Example { foo: 0, bar: format!("example formatted string"), baz: false, }; } fn struct_initialization_partial() { let object = Example { bar: format!("example formatted string"), ..Example::default() }; } fn builder_pattern() { // `ExampleBuilder` type not shown for brevity. let object = ExampleBuilder::default() .with_foo(123) .with_bar(format!("example formatted string")) .finish(); } But sometimes we want a different syntax than this, for readability reasons.Often custom syntaxes are only beneficial if there’s some common, well-accepted, pre-existing format (e.g. an existing data markup language, like JSON). But occasionally a purely custom syntax can be helpful.Containers are a great example of custom initialization syntax that everyone should have some experience with.It’s true you can (and should) implement FromIterator to initialize from some sequence of elements. But this syntax can be awkward for explicit initialization that isn’t coming from some already constructed values. So for developer convenience we often create small helper macros to improve readability.Like with many things relating to macros, only add them when you’re sure they’re useful. Think about whether the pre-existing methods for initializing objects is good enough.ExamplesIt should go without saying, but the vec! macro is a really popular example of this. And soon we will have yet another version of this, with the hash_map! macro.The best example of this I can think of for object initialization is the json! macro from the serde_json crate.This is actually a good example of using declarative macros to do something non-trivial. Specifically, note that they hide the implementation details of the macro by splitting it into multiple macros, json! is the main one you call, and it redirects to another exported macro which is hidden from documentation called json_internal.Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Sometimes you find yourself writing many similar lines of code within a small set of functions.In most cases, it’s best to just change these into helper functions and let the compiler optimize things. But sometimes you’ll run into situations where you can’t do that.You need to generate a distinct type per functional configuration (e.g. not just logic or impls).You’re using it to provide the body of a function that the macro is implementing, and you can’t generalize this function body over any trait bounds.When your macro influences the surrounding control flow (break, continue, return).For optimization reasons (which you have surely bench tested).Be careful when altering control flow.It can have some utility for really simple, localized helper macros. But I tend to consider it to be an anti-pattern to export such macros. However, used very sparingly, in unique cases to assist in implementing something, it can be helpful.Honestly, I even lean away from it for crate-local macros as well. Obfuscating the control flow negatively impacts readability in my experience.ExamplesOne example where this pattern being used for optimization reasons is within the Rust standard library. The str type specializes based on string lengths for optimization reasons (specialize_for_lengths; used here).The bytes crate actually uses some macros to reduce code duplication. See the crate-local buf_get_impl macro. This is a good example of the macro providing a common implementation for a set functions. The functions that are being implemented simply invoke the macro to expand this common implementation.An example of a crate-exported macro used to produce new types can be found in the bitflags crate. In this case, it uses some custom syntax that looks kind of like regular Rust code, so it’s a good reference for how to use some different fragment specifiers (like meta or vis).Finally, probably one of the most popular control-flow-impacting macros, is anyhow’s bail! macro. As mentioned, I’m not a fan of these kinds of macros (including this one). But I want to mention it anyway, since it fits within this set of example use-cases, and likely has some popularity. (Another potential example of this is the standard library’s ready! macro for polling futures.)A really simple example of this is constructing a newtype that redirects to the underlying implementation. We may want to ensure that the types are actually distinct from one another, but we may not want to re-implement the functionality the type provides (impl_displayable_type - example usage here - is an example of this from one of my own crates, typed-ident).// A simplified form of `impl_displayable_type` to use as an example. macro_rules! impl_displayable_type { ( name=$name:ident, over=$over:ident, docs=$docs:expr, ) => { #[doc = $docs] pub struct $name($over); impl core::fmt::Display for $name { #[inline] fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } }; } // We have some displayable types that we don't want to conflate. impl_displayable_type! { name = ObjectId, over = u64, docs = "Example documentation here", } impl_displayable_type! { name = GroupId, over = u64, docs = concat!( "`docs` is an expression so you can do things like this.\n", "\n", "Multi-line documentation, for better readability!", ), } // So now, if we have an API like this... struct Object; impl Object { pub fn object_id(&self) -> ObjectId { todo!() } pub fn group_id(&self) -> GroupId { todo!() } } // ... You can't accidentally do something like this. fn example_bad_usage_that_no_longer_compiles(object: Object) { let group_id: GroupId = object.object_id(); // Fails to compile! } It can be tempting to use declarative macros in places where a #[derive(...)] procedural macro would make more sense. Try to avoid creating such macros unless necessary.A common toy example for declarative macros is to create a function on enums so you can get static strings of the enum variant names. But this can be accomplished through a derive macro, and that feels more idiomatic to me (like IntoStaticStr from the strum crate, or - maybe better - having a custom trait to represent this).Do what you believe the end-user would find most natural. If what your macro is doing is implementing a trait - you probably ought to make it a derive macro unless you have good reason not to.We’ll talk more about derive macros when we cover procedural macros in a later article, though.

We may want to ensure that the types are actually distinct from one another, but we may not want to re-implement the functionality the type provides (impl_displayable_type - example usage here - is an example of this from one of my own crates, typed-ident).// A simplified form of `impl_displayable_type` to use as an example. macro_rules! impl_displayable_type { ( name=$name:ident, over=$over:ident, docs=$docs:expr, ) => { #[doc = $docs] pub struct $name($over); impl core::fmt::Display for $name { #[inline] fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } }; } // We have some displayable types that we don't want to conflate. impl_displayable_type! { name = ObjectId, over = u64, docs = "Example documentation here", } impl_displayable_type! { name = GroupId, over = u64, docs = concat!( "`docs` is an expression so you can do things like this.\n", "\n", "Multi-line documentation, for better readability!", ), } // So now, if we have an API like this... struct Object; impl Object { pub fn object_id(&self) -> ObjectId { todo!() } pub fn group_id(&self) -> GroupId { todo!() } } // ... You can't accidentally do something like this. fn example_bad_usage_that_no_longer_compiles(object: Object) { let group_id: GroupId = object.object_id(); // Fails to compile! } It can be tempting to use declarative macros in places where a #[derive(...)] procedural macro would make more sense. Try to avoid creating such macros unless necessary.A common toy example for declarative macros is to create a function on enums so you can get static strings of the enum variant names. But this can be accomplished through a derive macro, and that feels more idiomatic to me (like IntoStaticStr from the strum crate, or - maybe better - having a custom trait to represent this).Do what you believe the end-user would find most natural. If what your macro is doing is implementing a trait - you probably ought to make it a derive macro unless you have good reason not to.We’ll talk more about derive macros when we cover procedural macros in a later article, though.

#9905. Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare

Germany's Bundeswehr lifted precautionary grounding after malicious update reportedly reached military servers

Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding.

The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday.

"Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators."

It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years."

The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground.

The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution."

A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details.

Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years.

Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines.

Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

#9904. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9903. Reintroducing Spaces

Atproto Spaces are a new primitive in the atproto stack. We just launched the protocol in alpha. Check it out, give the blogpost a read, and sign up on the alpha PDS!

My own intuition around this protocol has been consistently evolving as I’ve worked on it. You can trace much of that through the Permissioned Data Diary series I wrote during the design process. Now with some time and perspective, I wanted to zoom back out, look at the design of Spaces and take a shot at succinctly motivating them as a new primitive.

Our initial goal was to extend atproto to work for non-public data. Specifically though, we wanted to enable social use cases. Which is to say that the protocol isn’t intended for just bookmarks or even “gated posts”, but needs to work for large multi-user social contexts such as a 100k user forum.

Our next goal is to maintain existing atproto intuition. Users publish records, those records are canonically stored in the user’s PDS, authority rests in the author’s DID, and applications crawl PDSes and sync data to build their own views. Succeeding in this means that many difficult questions around things like moderation and credible exit are already answered!

An extension of that goal is that it must be atmospheric. I use “atmospheric” to refer to the same underlying data getting remixed across apps in different lights. Think: Bluesky posts showing up as comments under a standard.site blog or rpg.actor characters walking across the bottom of your streamplace stream. Atmospheric features are the features that make this network feel like one deeply integrated experience rather than a bunch of isolated apps that just happen to have the same login.

And finally, the protocol needs to be secure and legible to users. This protocol enables many-to-many sharing in a multi-app, multi-pds, multi-modality network. That’s a lot of variables! This all comes to a head in the OAuth consent screen. And being able to communicate what an app is allowed to do in a concrete way in just a couple sentences is absolutely critical to the Atmosphere being broadly approachable and usable.

Spaces are our new primitive. Each space represents a shared social context. They’re a simple and concrete mechanism for organizing and permissioning data. Built around an abstraction of locality, each record is “in” a space and only one space. Each space is explicitly tied to a particular modality and owned by a single entity.

As we explored this new primitive, we realized that it seems uniquely able to thread the needle on all of our design goals.

Spaces are a deeply social primitive (fitting for a social networking protocol!). Spaces are not really about “who do I, as an individual, share this piece of content with”. Spaces are meant for establishing a shared social context. Records are in that context, and everyone with access to that context has the exact same view over it. It’s a shared common reality, and this shared sense of space allows for truly social applications.

We’ve started describing spaces as “mini atprotos” (btw if that sounds heavy duty, don’t worry spaces are actually very lightweight & low overhead). That analogy turns out to hold startlingly well. Not only does it help communicate the new primitive, but it also has the huge benefit that almost all of the really difficult questions of using the protocol for real-world social networks can be answered pretty simply: they’re the same as existing atproto! From moderation to account migration to the role of applications, intuition from public atproto maps very closely to spaces.

Spaces are quite legible. Of course this isn’t a gimme, the Atmosphere is pretty novel, and we’re all familiar with the new challenges of communicating this novel network to users. However, as I mentioned, this question of legibility comes to a head in the OAuth screen. In a context like that, describing “spaces” is much more grounded than trying to communicate ACLs or circles (as we’ll discuss in the next section).

One thing I didn’t expect when we started out designing spaces is how excited I would be for their applicability in public contexts as well. This realization partially underlies our shift in naming from “permissioned data protocol” to “atproto spaces”. This name shifts the focus from “who can see what” to locality. This new notion of locality is super handy and opens up all sorts of new options for data modeling. As a result of this locality, sync is also very lightweight and friendly. It felt so good to build my spaces example app and not have to comb through the entire global network. Locality in the sync protocol gave me exactly the data I needed.

To be upfront, the effect of designing spaces to be usable in multi-user social contexts is that they are less tailored towards permissioned publishing. Spaces are least tuned to the use case of publishing a bunch of individual pieces of content where each record has a different audience. If you realize that this seems like a weird approach to “I have a bunch of recipes and I want to share each with a totally different audience”, you’re not wrong! That use case was just not the primary design goal of atproto spaces.

That being said, I think spaces still work in that case. This deserves a blogpost & an example app of its own. However, a simple “out” for cases like this is to just put all your recipes in a space that you share with one or more applications and then let those applications manage the access logic.

In an effort to further bolster intuition around spaces, I also wanted to compare them to the most commonly-suggested alternate approach. I broadly refer to this approach as “Circles” (after Google+ Circles).

Circles: the content is the object, audience is an attribute you attach to it. You write a post, then tag it with who can see it.

Spaces: space is the object, content is published into it. A post goes "into" a space and is viewable by anyone with access to the space.

Circles come in many forms. The simplest is just “putting ACLs on records”. Once you start enabling large multi-user social use cases like forums, you realize you need to share the same ACL across many records owned by many users. Now you have a circle!

In their fullest forum, circles can be created by anyone, re-used by anyone, and apply to any data. For example, my friend can create the circle “Besties” and I can share recipes, blogposts, and videos with that circle.

However, softer versions of circles include arguments that records should be able to be in more than one space. Once you change this invariant, a record is no longer “in” a space. The record “exists” (outside of any given space), and then each space is attached as metadata, giving the record visibility in that space. We’re back to circles!

Circles seem simple at first pass, and they’re are many folks’ first instinct for social permissioning (including mine!). However they hide a lot of complexity. For one, there’s a lot of cognitive overhead, juggling who’s in which circle and which content is shared with whom. And thinking through the repercussions of sharing a post with multiple circles is difficult to understand. For instance, if I share with my “Family” and my “Besties” circles, are they able to see each other’s comments and likes?

All of this complexity gets dramatically exacerbated in the multi-app, multi-pds, multi-modality network that I described earlier.

I have a claim, which I’ll (cheekily) call Daniel’s Circles Postulate:

To quickly get the intuition behind this claim, consider that “Besties” circle from before (different account & different modality). If I upload a video with my video app and share it with Besties, my friend (who created the circle) can use his recipe app to change the access perimeter on my video. Not only does this violate all rules and intuition about resource ownership, but even if it is actually what you intend to do, I have no earthly idea how you would make those side-effects legible to either of the users involved or go about communicating that capability in the recipe app’s OAuth screen.

In short, the Atmosphere is a very dynamic network, there are a lot of variables at play. In this flux, I believe we benefit by having a deeply social, grounded, and concrete primitive that orders our interaction model. I don’t believe that any variation on circles (ACLs, the full fluid expression, or just allowing records to surface in multiple spaces) gives that to us.

So please give it a go! Check out the recent blogpost for directions on how to get started with the alpha, or just head over to the new BPS site to get your invite code for the alpha PDS.

Please let me know your thoughts! Share what you build. Let me know what works, and let me know what doesn’t. What’s confusing, what’s a pain to do, what breaks.

I can’t express enough how much I appreciate all the feedback along the way, so please keep it coming. I really believe this protocol is going to be critical for the Atmosphere, so we need to make sure it’s something we’re all excited about building on.

Let’s build the future of the internet :)

#9902. Oh my Word! Microsoft retires compatibility options, because who needs layouts to stay put

Admins with archives of ancient files brace for the wave of tickets from confused users

Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier.

"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said.

The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change."

Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it.

Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms."

Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put.

The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027.

Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite.

Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well. Losing some of those safeguards could give administrators a fresh batch of "what the heck has happened to this document?" tickets as the change rolls out. ®
