#9848. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector

Hannes Hapke shares how Dataiku’s open-source Kiji Inspector applies Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) directly to decision tokens to expose why agents pick specific tools. Moving past superficial chain-of-thought narratives, he discusses causal ablation, layer activation extraction via patched vLLM engines, and production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

For today, we want to focus on what we call the Kiji Inspector. It is a tool that is helping you to understand how agents "Think." The fundamental problem that we have with agents is that we don't know how they actually make their decisions. We have a number of tools out there. We have prompt engineering, behavioral testing, or probably the most sophisticated processes like chain of thought. None of them are actually providing you causality, they're often just giving you plausible explanations or plausible narratives of what the root cause could be. When we were asked to figure out how can we make sure that the model that is running an agent is picking the right tool, how do we know that it's thinking about the right context, we decided that we needed to look into the model.

The way we do this is by using sparse autoencoders. Before we get there, let me start explaining what an autoencoder is. This is a concept that has been around for a very long time, probably three decades by now. Autoencoders take a set of inputs, reduce this to a smaller latent space vector, and then reconstruct them through a decoder. The whole point of that autoencoder is that you want to minimize the error between the input and the reconstructed output. In an optimal system, there would be zero error, and the output here would be exactly as the input. Then you know that the representation of your vector z here in your latent space is most optimal. This has been used many times in various things like embeddings and vector searches and information compression, dimensionality reductions of various sorts of kinds. This is a really interesting way of forcing your model to reduce the amount of information to a smaller vector space.

The cool thing about this concept is that it's self-supervised. You don't need any labeling. You use the input as the output, that's your target, and then in between, that's what you would use in production. With sparse autoencoders, you would flip this concept around a little bit. Here in this case, we wouldn't create a bottleneck for the information, but we want to go wide here, with a little catch, and I'll explain the catch. Let's say you grab an activation from a model, or a hidden state, and you pass it through the sparse autoencoder, you can go wide in the information, and that means you force the model to pick certain features to represent the information. When you take a look at the activations inside of a model, there's something that we call polysemantic representation of the context, which means that one neuron that fires can have multiple meanings or topics it would fire on.

In our feature representation, if we want to understand the model, we need to separate them and put them apart from each other, and so that's why we're going wide in the feature representations here. Then again, we try to then have a decoder where we narrow that information piece again, and we try to reconstruct the activations that we used as an input. The catch here is that in this activation function, we are then forcing the model to only use a small set of features to be actually active, and the rest of them, roughly 95%, that's the ideal number, we want to force them to be zero. In that moment, we actually force the model during the training process to just be really selective on a handful of features, and then we can be absolutely certain that those features are representing the themes and the context of the model itself, what the model was thinking in this given layer at the processing of a certain token.

Then we can go one step further. Once you have those feature vectors you generated, those indices don't mean anything to us, to humans. What we can then do is, once we have a corpus, we can grab all the documents that fire highly on, let's say, dimension 3 and dimension 6, and then we can look at those documents and say, what do they have in common? It could easily be that they say like, the first one has something to do with Python, so then over the course of the entire corpus, we could say, those two features, they represent a programming language or an API vocabulary or things like this.

What we have tried to do in this project is combining a number of things and package them up so that everybody can use them in production. The first thing that we want to do is, sparse autoencoders have been around for a number of years now, and OpenAI published some research, and Eleuther published some research on this, but they focused on the entire LLM generation. What we changed here in our approach is we were only interested in the agentic decision-making. We focused on the decision token rather than the entire prompt, and then averaging those activations across the entire prompt. Then we put a bunch of concepts together. For example, Eleuther came out with this concept of token-level fuzzing, and so we added this to our framework so anybody who wants to use that framework and trains their own models, they can use that token testing. Then also we added causal validation testing as well so that you can make sure, is it actually causal or is it just correlation?

Then the other sweet thing, what we changed here in this project, what is novel, is that we're not just training on a number of prompts, but we created those pairs, training pairs. We have a given intent — I'll show you an example later — but for a given intent, you have something that we call the anchor that's the correct answer and the correct tool use, and then there's an adversarial reply, which is very similar, but very different. It's basically like look something up in an internal database versus look up something online. Two different use cases, very similar in the prompt response, but very different outcome in terms of the tool selection.

Looking at the training pipeline, let's say we have all these pairs generated, which I will show you how we do this. We then take our target model, and little caveat here, those have to be open-source models. We can't do this with OpenAI's models because we don't have access to their weights, but you can do this with any open-source model, and that's another novelty in our framework that we're not just focusing on Gemma models from Google or Nemotron models from NVIDIA. That tool, that framework here is working with various open-source models that are out there. You pick your subject model, that's the model you want to use the explainability for, and then you run all your prompts through the model itself, grab all the activations from the particular layers you want to watch. Then with those activations, you can train your sparse autoencoder as I just showed you with putting them in, widening them up, and then forcing the decoder again to reconstruct that activation.

Then once you have the model trained, you can do a contrastive analysis, and I'll show you this later, how we then figure out through those pairs of what's actually relevant in the context or not. Or you can go to a large language model and say, tell me what those documents have in common, and then you can generate those themes. This all happens in that package where we call the Kiji Inspector. You put in your corpus, you nominate those models, and out you get a feature definition of what those features mean when you run those LLMs and agent requests.

Earlier, I just mentioned you have to pick a certain layer. There's a little bit of an art what layer to pick rather than science. There's a little bit of an explanation here that if you're early in the stack, like maybe in the first third, the model hasn't fully conceptualized all the concepts of your prompt request. You're basically activating things that are highly relevant to the prompt itself. If you're further down the stack, there's a lot of intricacies of the model itself. Here in this particular model, we're looking at the Nemotron 3 from NVIDIA. That's an MoE model. That's because every different request goes through different routings, you have crazy errors. Learning something later on is very difficult. Also, the concepts you extract are so abstract in some cases that even for humans, it's impossible to understand what's going on. Then also for the models, it's difficult.

What we wanted to do is, for our particular experiments, we picked layer 20 because it is already down the pipe. It's like the model extracted some abstract concepts. It's not too far down the pipe that it would be too non-human understandable. In our open-source models, what we're publishing, we're publishing multiple layers. You can pick wherever you want to be in your model layer setup. Again, this is another representation of the training pipeline. Basically, you have your input. You calculate those representations. Then you do the reconstruction back to, in our case, it's 2688 dimensions. Then you calculate the loss. It's a very standard autoencoder model architecture. The key thing, and we show this in the following slide, we're using a particular activation, what we call the Jump Regularized Linear Unit. I will explain this here why this is in this particular case.

Then, how do we actually focus on the decision token? The way we do this is by forcing the agent to respond to a given prompt and says, I will use blank. Whatever tool, whatever the model then responds is expected to be the tool name, because we've provided the selection of tools in the prompt itself. Then in the response, we would see what tool the model has chosen. We do this a million times. We generated a training set with a million samples, basically 500,000 pairs, good and bad examples. The pairs come in later when we try to evaluate the model. During the training process itself, we use them raw, and we have those 1 million samples. Why are we doing this contrastive pair design again? Here's a little example. Let's say you have a given intent, resolve a password issue, and you can have the request, how do I reset my password?

That would trigger the tool knowledge base. You could also say, I tried to reset my password three times, and that could be a completely different tool. It's very similar in the response or in the request, but it's a very different tool outcome in this particular case. Later on, what you will see is we will then use those pairs and figure out which of the features we generated are actually relevant for those given tools. When we generate the features for both tools, the dimensions where the features are different have mostly contributed to the decision-making between knowledge base versus ticket lookup.

I don't want to go through the math here, but there's an interesting concept regarding the JumpReLU. As you know, Regularized Linear Units basically are, anything negative is zeroed out and anything positive is the input. It's like a linear function, but it's not differentiable because of that bend. Here in the JumpReLU, that's another derivative of the ReLU activation function. It's basically the output is the input, but there's a threshold. The interesting thing here is when we train the model of, figure out which activation is actually relevant and not relevant, we can then tune that threshold during the training process as the output activation. That's another tweak we can have to teach the model which feature is relevant for which given activation. When we look at some results per layer, then we see some really interesting side effects of early on, the error is low, but the model hasn't learned much.

Later on, the error is crazy high because this is logarithmic. Then we have too many, basically we learn something, but the error is exorbitant high. That's why we ended up in our practical example, we ended up somewhere in between at layer 20. Again, if we look at some stats here, like total, I think we had like 2,600-and-something input features, we widened this to 10,000 dimensions. Of those 10,000 dimensions, a little bit above 80% of those dimensions are alive. That means somewhere through the training, they have been nonzero. Then only less than 0.2% are completely dead, meaning those features have never been used through the entire training process. Then when we do the testing later on, we actually figured out that out of those 10,000 features, 668 are actually highly relevant to all the tool selections we wanted to investigate. This is for a given model for a given layer and a given dataset. If you retrain this, you might see different results.

Then somebody could say, why do we have to go through all this craziness of sparse autoencoders and training another machine learning model in all these crazy setups? As you can imagine, it's a lot of computation there. This is basically a couple comparisons. If you take the activations and then train a linear model on this, could we then figure out is this tool correct or incorrect? If you compare this and a binary classification here, we get to almost 80% accuracy. It's not bad, but it's also not perfect. Then if you do some just accuracy versus F1 score, that's a little bit lower. Then somebody could say, what happens if we just take those activations with those 2,000 dimensions and we just cluster them? Could we from the cluster then figure out which tool is the correct one? You're better off flipping a coin than actually clustering.

I think that was for us the interesting thing to see with the sparse autoencoders. I'll explain what fuzzing is. We can bridge the gap between interpretability and also having some causality testable features. I just mentioned token-level fuzzing. That was introduced by Eleuther sometime back when they looked into sparse autoencoders for entire prompts. What they did was they took a look at the prompt and then swapped out individual tokens, and then looked at how is the activation affected by swapping out those tokens and how is the end result being affected by that. That's the same concept we provide in our tool case here, in our framework that people can use when they want to evaluate their sparse autoencoders. Then when you look at the individual features and the quality of them, we can see that for the majority of the features they actually correlate really well to what we predicted the outcome to be. Only a small number of them have very poor influence on the overall decision-making. Again, from those 600 features we selected, it felt pretty good. This is heading in the right direction.

Then, let's take a look at causality and those other things. That's always the big question. We started this project where like, can we explain how an agent selected a tool? At some point, we needed to take a look at, can we actually prove causality? Little side note, I'm not a statistician, so I would love to have a better conversation about this with somebody who is more experienced with this. What we have done is looking at the activations. While the activation in this given layer in the model was produced, we then zeroed out the top 10 activations in that given vector. Then we looked at, is the tool selection changing or not? This was our setup. It's a little bit of like wiring and intercepting all the activations and those types of things. Don't worry, through the framework, we provide the other tools where you can replicate that.

The way this works is for our experiment setups here, where we looked at various tools, we were actually able to show that if you do the contrastive ablation, that worked extremely well for a number of tools. There were certain tools where we couldn't prove it, but for the majority of the tools, it actually looked very promising. Just a couple results here, the p-score is very low, so we were pretty happy about this. Through those testing, we were able to show that 23 of those contrast types actually worked. That worked better than randomly flipping. We felt that this is also, again, heading in the right direction. Like, yes, those particular activations, those 10 dimensions we blanked out or zeroed out actually contributed actively to the tool selection.

This was a lot of theory and a little bit of math and all those types of things, but you don't have to do this yourself, and that's why we have the Kiji Inspector, and that's why we open sourced that at Dataiku. What we're trying to provide here with a toolkit and the framework is like, we wanted to provide a model-agnostic framework that everybody else can use in the industry. Companies like Google have published similar frameworks, but they're always very tool specific. For example, Gemma Scope is the explainability tool for Gemma 2 or Gemma 3 or Gemma 4, or there's no Gemma 4 expanded model yet. There is no training pipeline. There's a lot of repos floating around with scripts and everything, but it's not like something you can download and fork and run something end-to-end on your site for your particular models and your particular use cases.

Then we wanted to provide a full production setup. We see a lot of research in those cases, but we hadn't seen a good production setup where people can run vLLMs and also get the activations back. Because in most setups like vLLM or SGLang, you get the response back but those inference tools don't give you the activations of a particular layer back. We provide a patch to vLLM that allows you to do that, and we also give you the containers so you can run this in production. Then as I said, everything is fully open source. We provide Docker containers, there's a PyPI package as you will see, and then all the models we have trained are on Hugging Face. This is only a subset, the list is way longer of what we're providing on Hugging Face. With our large training set of those 1 million data points or 1 million samples and the 500,000 pairs, we recently just trained Gemma 4.

Who knows if Google actually comes out with their sparse autoencoders. We wanted to beat them, and so we have the sparse autoencoders for the Gemma 4 and then for the latest Nemotron models, the Nemotron 3, we also provide the sparse autoencoders. Unfortunately, we don't have infinite compute resources as Google, that's why we have to pick certain layers to support them. If you have specific reasons, and you want a particular layer of a particular model, let us know, we can probably help you there as well.

How would the inference setup look like? If you run for example an agent and says, analyze my Q3 report, you would go through a large language model. Again, it has to be an open-source model, because you have to host that model so you can patch your vLLM version. We're hoping to get this into vLLM at some point so that hosting platforms like Baseten and others can provide those features as well. Then, you not just get the response back but you also get the activation vector for a given layer for your response. Then that goes into your sparse autoencoder. From your 2688 dimensions, you would then go up to 10,000 dimensions. Remember most of the dimensions are actually zero. Then you can take a look at the top features that are active in this large vector, and then you can take a look at those indices and figure out what are the themes you have determined during the training itself.

Then you can take those themes and put them back into a large language model as an explanation. Now somebody might ask, what's the difference now between doing all of this and chain of thought? The key difference is this information piece was directly derived from the activation during the model when that token was generated. It is not chain of thought where it first goes through some reasoning steps and then tries to execute. In chain of thought it could say like, here are two things I want to do, and then it executes 15 other things. There's no connection between those two steps. Here, there's the direct connection between the activation at a given layer. It goes into the sparse vector, and then we have the connection to the feature map we generated during the training.

Now the actually fun part starts. In Hugging Face, you can define what we call forward hooks. When the model is being executed, in Hugging Face the model is not compiled so you can easily hook into the execution, and say, give me the vector of a given layer for that given input. Then, we can grab the layer from here. When it's being executed, we can then actually ship it back to the response and send it to the user. I can show you another setup we have where you can also work with compiled models so you get a better performance. Then you run the inference, you retrieve the vector, and that is your activation. You're ready to go to use your sparse autoencoder. If you use one of the models we already support, you can then use our Kiji Inspector. We followed the Hugging Face setup. You can say like, from pre-trained, you mention the base model and under the hood we figure out like, what sparse autoencoder it needs to download.

We go to the correct repo, and then we use the correct model for the correct layer. Under the hood we convert this into the correct feature vector and then also do the lookup of the features to the themes. When you run SAE describe, that's how you get the description and not just a random vector. This is how it looks like, and I will show you this, again, but this is a little bit better readable. You see all the indices up here, they basically tell you what indices is the top five the ones that are firing. You see the number one it says unknown. What does it mean? It means like during the training, that feature in that feature vector was not of high importance and we haven't described that. Maybe we need more training data or maybe we need to tweak the training process. The interesting thing is that when we look at the second feature that was firing, it was actually something related to dishwasher gasket issues.

Seems relevant to the prompt we have. If it would fire on something completely unrelated here then there would be a good sign to go back and say like, maybe there's something going on in the model or maybe my prompt is incorrect or something else happening. Those are the things you can then see from the inspection and the data we provide through the package.

Let me show you here a little demo of how this would work and how you can actually use this in production. Again, this is the same code that I showed you earlier where we just stepped through. I pre-ran this in a Colab notebook. If you want to follow along you can go to our GitHub repo. The quick start example works in a free Colab. If you want to use a larger model you have to pay for the bigger GPUs nowadays. This is still giving you an overview of how this works under the hood. Here's a truncated information on the slide. You see some more information, and we also provide the bottom examples. Basically, here you see all the things that are least related to that request. Then you can go down, and you can turn this into a description and you can see what the confidence level is.

Here's another thing that I think could be really interesting for folks. As I mentioned at the beginning, we provide patches for vLLM. Here in this case is like you can also execute the whole thing in vLLM. When you do vLLM generate, you can then also get the same vectors back with the explanations. We tied this all together in vLLM. Then we have another interesting example I think that is a use case where we're stepping through a larger agent setup. Instead of going through the code I want to show you how the result could look like, and maybe that gives you a feeling of how you can use this in your product. We built the standalone demo of like, this is your home repair agent. It tells you if something is broken, can you fix it yourself? Should you call somebody else? It could potentially look up YouTube videos of how to fix it.

In order to make sure that we know what the agent is doing, for every agent step, we then also look up what the sparse autoencoder features are. Here in this particular case, this was the dishwasher example, it relates to a machine handling water I would think, washing machines, and there's something like old machine troubling. At least we know that the agent is heading in the right direction when it made the decision of like a dishwasher is leaking in this particular case. You can do this for every different tool call. This one is completely empty, it's a good example, because when we trained this there was not a tool call in the training set at all for YouTube videos. For us it will be a good sample of like, we need to add more real-world examples in our training set. I showed you this example. There's a couple more, there's a left example there as well where we show this in a live demo, you can follow along what the agent is doing in the frontend while the agent is figuring out what is actually happening. It's pretty fun to look at.

What are the particular use cases you can use for your applications and where you could use the Kiji Inspector. One thing is like you could figure out what an agent misbehavior would be. Anything that is like, has it picked the wrong tool, as I showed you earlier in the examples, that is a something. You can do it for audit compliance. Some companies looking at this and figuring out, it's like, if we have another track record, traces is one thing but explainability is another thing. When we do traces, we basically see what tool has been selected but we still can't explain why that tool was selected. Here we generate another set of logs and figuring out why the agent has particularly selected this tool that is shown in the traces. Then we can do validate of prompt engineering. If you're not quite sure, like you want to optimize your prompt for particular goals and you don't want to do this iterative loop, you can then also investigate like how is that tool responding to your given prompt based on the activations.

Then obviously monitoring production drift. If your data changes, let's say you test your agent with a set of prompts, you watch those activations, and then over time you can see if those activations change. That is a really good indication that the data that is going through that agent has changed. Maybe you should take a look at that as well.

Just to summarize this, what are the key takeaways? We have the chance to prove that sparse autoencoders can work to explain why the agent made a certain decision. We showed how the token-level fuzzing works, and as part of the package we can prove that tweaking those prompts lead to different activations. I also showed the causal evidence of the tool selection is affected by zeroing out certain activations in the model itself. Then we did some comparison with construction only baseline, meaning, because it's a decoder and there's a loss effect, if we take this out, then we can actually show that there's a causal effect in the sparse autoencoder.

I want to let you go with a couple limitations and also pointing out some future work. As I said, you do need the model itself. It doesn't work with closed source models. Hopefully at some point they give us similar tools on there, and that would be fantastic. The training is pretty compute intensive, especially if you want to create your own datasets. If you want to use the tool and you want to create your own training sets, come talk to us. We can share some more tricks and tips of how to run this effectively. As I mentioned earlier, it is a synthetic dataset. If anybody wants to use this and has some ideas of what is missing in the dataset and where should we go in terms of making it more real-world replicable, then let us know. We would love to collaborate on that as well.

There's a future work here. We want to support more open-source models and provide those models from the start through Hugging Face. Something that is on mind is currently Qwen. More multi-layer experiments. Currently everything is based on single layers. It could be really interesting if you take a layer from the first third and then a layer from the last third, and then combine those and see what actually happens. Then another interesting idea we had was like what happens if you do cross-model transfer. Basically, you train on a Gemma model. You take those vectors. You learn certain features. Is there something we can generalize then if we go to another model and so we see certain patterns. That is all future work. We haven't touched this yet. If anybody wants to collaborate on this let me know. Everything is fully open source. We live from contribution from others. This is not our project. It's a community project.

Participant 1: Is there anything that stops this from being applied to something by the training, of course, beyond tool calls. For example, if we were looking at safety alignment. The reason being that at least from the results of the causal inspection that you did, it seems to be possible to do some kind of steering after you train the model. Do you have any insight on any ways that we could possibly change something like this for alignment and then use that for active steering after deployment.

Hannes Hapke: I think there's nothing that I would say that it's not possible. One of the things we're looking into is the security aspects of like, can we detect malicious attacks in those activations? Yes, I think that's possible. I think from the research I showed earlier when I showed the clustering versus linear classification versus the sparse autoencoder, it was visible to me. I think to me that's sort of the proof that if you just look at their pure activations you can't figure out what is going on. You do need the step through the sparse autoencoder. Yes, nothing is limited to just a tool call. For us, it was like a feasible project scope. The team is pretty small, so for us it felt feasible. Yes, totally.

Participant 2: Do you have any real-world examples where using your approach gave you a different understanding of why a tool was selected versus using chain of thought tells?

Hannes Hapke: Yes, we have a bunch of anecdotal examples. We haven't summarized them yet into something scientific that we say here's my prompt and here's my analysis. Chain of thought was maybe a bit abstract. Then in the features, we could see like, this is actually looking for a particular problem. For example, this dishwasher repair thing, it picked water damage on an electrical equipment or something. It felt more precise than the actual chain of thought. There's a little caveat. The sparse autoencoder we trained for those examples, they were domain specific. Meaning that we were focusing on a very particular specific domain and that's what we built the training set for. There was a little bit of an unfair advantage. Also, it changes with model size. If you use a smaller model like the Gemma E4B, I think those interpretability tools have a benefit of it. Those were the two things where you could see the difference between the chain of thought versus the explainability tool.

Participant 2: For those who are stuck with the closed source proprietary models, could you imagine surrogate models working ok enough? Do you think that the closed and open-source models are similar enough with why they would make certain choices?

Hannes Hapke: I can't speak for OpenAI and others. I would think the models are bigger than what we see in the open-source world obviously. I think you have maybe a better chain of thought experiments. That's an interesting question. We should compare different prompts and run them through a large Qwen model versus a large like OpenAI 5.5, and then look at the thinking steps, and see, are they comparable or not? Generally, we will never see this technology in closed source models, because, A, I think all the companies are walking back their logics now, because through the logics you could figure out model internals. This is even more like internals. They never want to share this. The other thing is also like, yes, it's proprietary modeling. They don't want to really open source that or share that.

#9844. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9843. [$] C++26 contract confusion

The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has blessed seven C++ language revisions since 1998. The language is mostly developed by ISO's Working Group 21, which considers proposed additions and amendments, integrates them into a document, and then presents that document to the main ISO body to be voted on as a standard. On October 23, for the first time ever, ISO declined to ratify a document presented by Working Group 21, leaving the future of the C++26 standard in doubt. The decision was driven by controversy around a proposed new "contracts" feature that would add pre- and post-conditions to function signatures.

#9842. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9841. Introducing Polo: a Wayland MATE compositor

Kerem Söke has announced the 1.0 release of Polo, a Wayland compositor for the MATE Desktop Environment:

The idea is to keep MATE behaving as closely as possible to how it does on X11, rather than changing the desktop to fit a different compositor. [...]

Window management, metacity, workspaces, tiling, XWayland, clipboard and clipman support, multiple monitors, display scaling, hotplugging, screenshots, screen sharing, and session management are all working.

I've also added desktop effects: fade, zoom, zap, spin, squeemize, magic lamp, desktop cube, expo, and wobbly windows.

Söke is looking for people to test Polo, particularly on multi-monitor setups, and report back with problems.

InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read

Technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.

Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:

If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.

Debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our new learning.

Debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.

Yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:

Every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.

The challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao said. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.

Technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we update our understanding, Yao explained:

The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.

AI introduces a new challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.

Agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.

InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?

Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.

Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.

InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?

Yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.

A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

#9839. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9838. Glasswing overwhelms maintainers with underwhelming findings (VulnCheck)

Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck has written a blog post that looks at vulnerabilities found by Anthropic's Project Glasswing since it launched on April 7, and finds it wanting:

Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as "True Positives".

[...] AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

So I'm not super surprised if not many of 40,000 potential security bugs have actually made it to "really fixed" yet.

Unusual/stale? Posted Nov 12, 2026 22:17 UTC (Thu) by Vorpal (guest, #136011) [Link] (1 responses) This very much matches my experience at my dayjob as well. For patch code review LLMs can be really good, with some false positives (but quite few). They find things (most) humans would never think about, especially about interactions with entirely different parts of the code base. That said, they also miss things humans wouldn't, for example about overall system design. And, as you said, the author generally have the code fresh in their mind making it easy to deal with the feedback. We have also tried finding security issues with LLMs and there it was much more of a mixed bag. A few were genuine bugs, but many of those weren't actually security issues or even worth fixing (e.g. "yes this is a theoretical bug in things we are sending, if you assume another part of the same application building on top of this staticly linked library is actively malicious, and since this is C++, almost everything assumes the API user isn't 'holding it wrong'."). And a fair share were straight up incorrect. And of course, typically no one knows exactly what the code does off the top of their heads (some parts of the code even date to the late 90s), so triaging takes way more time than dealing with feedback on a PR. It is interesting to me that LLMs does so much poorly in one area than another. Unusual/stale? Posted Nov 13, 2026 16:38 UTC (Fri) by rgmoore (✭ supporter ✭, #75) [Link] It is interesting to me that LLMs does so much poorly in one area than another. It doesn't seem that surprising to me. Patches are smaller and should be easier to reason about. They're also likely to be way buggier than established code, so there are just more real bugs to find. I bet you'd have the same general trend if you ran the LLM bug finding on established projects. Before AI, people were trusting random stuff online way too much. You can be unlucky and meet bad people in real life but the chances are reasonably low because most people are decent. So trusting by default statistically works in real life - and that's great (Assuming you still have a "real life". I digress.) Even when we know it, we keep forgetting that these statistics are skewed online and the ratio is totally different there because the "global village" connectivity enables all the scammers and propagandists in the world to easily find you and engage with you - unlike in real life. But before AI there were still a few practical limits, even online. So people were still falling for it. Now thanks to AI, those practical limits are gone. So now the majority of what's unsolicited and/or strange online is genuinely suspicious and I think the misguided "trust by default" is finally dying there. About time. Now everyone is starting to educate themselves, realize that "they are the product" if it's free, demand proper security, reputation systems, ... - all safety things they should all have done a long time ago. There is still a long way to go: the safety and security systems still suck, many people still trust too much, monopolies, enshittification, ... but online naivety seems to be (slowly) going down? Good riddance. Some of the current AI backslash might also be caused to that. I mean not just caused by energy, water, inflation and layoffs but also by the increase of online garbage. This is a good instance of "It must get worse before it gets better". Or some sort of "tradegy of the commons" for bad guys? Who knows, this might even get people to spend less time online?

I wasn't including "online media", I was only referring to _unknown and unsolicited_ media. Whether you are consuming Fox News or the New York Times, it's really not hard to verify that you are really consuming those and not some impersonation. That particular problem is basically solved. Once you have verified that what you see actually came from Fox News or the New York Times and you know who's talking (first, critical _identification_ step), then should you _trust_ them? (second step) Trusting _identified_ sources is a very different question that I wasn't touching on. Because the answer is the same that it's always has been: 1. Find who pays them (often: not you!) 2. Count the number of mistakes, lies and contradictions over long periods of time. 3. Shortcut: ask people you trust who have been doing that work. That is how trust always gets built: with transitive reputation and over time. There is nothing new in those second step, trust processes, the global village and AI did not change anything and do not matter here. If people starting trusting _random_ stuff less and less thanks to AI garbage as I'm hoping in the previous comment, then the "traditional", pre-Internet trust systems will hopefully start working better again. Cause the former has been leveraging our confirmation bias and other bad instincts to actively harm the latter. With long and deep enough observation you can gauge not just the reliability when reporting facts but also the bias when expressing opinions. Assuming there is a clear distinction between the two in the first place - if not then run. You must constantly monitor the reliability of your shortcuts/friends/gurus too. Confirmation bias is an even higher risk there. Good education teaches that too. > how can you verify anything anymore ? You can't always verify everything yourself. That's why trust (and of course: free speech) exist. One thing I like to do is to read articles that teach me nothing on a topic I'm already very familiar with: great way to assert reliability. For instance: computer stuff in mainstream media.

#9836. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.
