#9835. Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Most organizations haven't sorted out their cryptographic estate enough to even know where they'd start with post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

The pressure is mounting for security leaders to get serious about their post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition plans, but most organizations aren't even ready to get ready for PQC.

Studies show that, yes, CISOs today do see PQC as a priority they've got to plan for. However, the bulk of organizations don't have a detailed enough cryptographic inventory to help them sketch out a roadmap of where to get started.

"When it comes to post-quantum cryptography, every company, no matter which ones you talk to are kind of stuck in the discovery phase," says Dr. Anurag Swarnim Yadav, founder and CTO of the startup QubitAC.

Recent numbers back up his observations. According to a July study by DigiCert, while 87% of organizations say they're planning, testing, or implementing PQC, only 44% have developed transition plans or created inventories. That mirrors another study by Ponemon Institute that found only 43% of organizations have full visibility of their cryptographic estate. Those respondents reported that their inability to discover those assets and improve that visibility is their number one greatest concern about PQC migration.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Cryptography sits in web servers, certificates, VPNs, code signing, vendor products and all nature of assets in between. Getting every encryption use case ready for a post-quantum world will be a sweeping transition, and the latest research suggests developments in quantum computing are proceeding on a much faster timeline than originally anticipated. If an enterprise can't enumerate all the cryptography impacted, it means they're not toeing the start line for this footrace.

Getting all of those assets into post-quantum readiness will be a generational effort easily on par with the Y2K effort. Unlike with Y2K, however, there's no set-in-stone deadline for post-quantum.

The closest thing is Q Day, the point when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) can break the public-key cryptography behind key exchange and digital signatures. The big problem with building a widespread sense of urgency is that nobody knows exactly when Q Day will arrive.

Yadav says estimates for when Q Day will come run from 2030 to 2040 and beyond, but his own bet is that attackers could pull it off by 2029 based how the research is shifting. The expected window until Q Day arrives keeps compressing as quantum researchers perfect their craft. Last year, Google researchers calculated that breaking 2048-bit RSA encryption would take a quantum computer 20 times smaller than they had estimated in 2019. And in March Google set a 2029 target for its own PQC migration, influenced by such research and recent progress in quantum hardware.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

Global governments are also starting to get firm about their own timing expectations for PQC transition in the run-up to Q Day. NIST finalized its PQC transition roadmap in late October, and a June executive order requires federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to move key establishment to post-quantum algorithms by 2030 and digital signatures by 2031. The United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre recommends that large organizations complete discovery and assessment and build an initial migration plan by 2028, then finish migrating by 2035.

Even if we don’t know exactly when Q Day will come about, the math behind what will happen after that day is well understood. Public-key cryptography lets two parties who have never met agree on a secret and prove who they are. It works because some math is easy to run forward and impractical to reverse. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring huge numbers, while elliptic curve cryptography and Diffie-Hellman key exchange rely on a related problem called the discrete logarithm.

Quantum computers use subatomic particles instead of transistors to represent data. This gives them an edge in how they process the ones and zeros of computing. Cryptography experts for years have warned that a sufficiently advanced enough quantum computer could use that edge to factor huge numbers and solve discrete logarithms at a rate of efficiency unheard of from even the most advanced classical super computers.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

There's also a more immediate deadline that's brewing from what attackers are likely doing today to prepare for Q Day. It's fairly trivial for the bad guys to vacuum up high-value encrypted traffic today with the promise that they might have a chance to decrypt it at a later date. For long-lived information like financial or health details, or secret sauce intellectual property, the long-game of this harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) is worth the effort for future-minded criminals.

"The data is worthless to attackers right now, but becomes priceless later," Yadav explains. He offers credit card numbers as a classic example. They stay valid for years, so a cache of encrypted numbers harvested now could still be good if Q Day lands inside that window.

In its recently finalized roadmap, the National Institute of Standards and Technology named HNDL as one of the main reasons the transition is so urgent. NIST mathematician and cryptographic expert Andrew Regenscheid says HNDL reframes the whole PQC timeline for critical information stores across industry and government systems.

"This information may need to remain secret for years, or even decades, into the future," he explained in a NIST Q&A this summer. "For that kind of information, waiting until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives is waiting too long."

Considering that the most isolated cryptographic migrations can still linger for upwards of a decade or longer, even a conservative 2040 estimate for Q Day should be enough to have security experts scrambling to plan PQC transitions. The scale of changes needed will take significant planning and prioritization that will need to be phased in.

"Changing these algorithms is something that’s been done before. It’s a complex process that takes years," Regenscheid said. "Based on our experience and the challenge of navigating the post-quantum world, we expect this process to be the most challenging one yet. The breadth of these systems and the complexity of the change will dwarf what we’ve done before."

The destination, at least, is defined. In 2024, NIST finalized three post-quantum standards, one for key exchange (ML-KEM) and two for digital signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA), built on math that's expected to hold up against quantum computers. The harder job is finding every place RSA and elliptic curve cryptography still run, and planning how and when to swap out each use case. Because of HNDL, NIST suggests the first transition phases should be prioritized around data that is particularly sensitive or has to stay secure for a long time.

In a September study on PQC readiness, Frost & Sullivan analysts emphasized how important risk-based prioritization like this will be for PQC readiness.

"A non-compliant cryptographic asset supporting a low-value application may represent limited immediate risk, while the same technology supporting sensitive information or a critical business process could require urgent remediation," they wrote.

Sorting through all the assets and ranking them depends on having a solid inventory on hand, though. This is why the discovery is so crucial. Frost &Sullivan concurred that the discovery process is proving to be trickier than many thought it would be.

"The inventory needs to extend beyond simply identifying algorithms to understanding the dependencies between cryptographic assets and business-critical applications," they explained.

Tools — commercial and open source — designed to assist organizations in their PQC journey are already available. These tools have their own approaches and have varying levels of maturity. One such tool is AC Scanner, which Yadav and QubitAC co-founder Joseph Wilson demoed at Black Hat Arsenal last August. The free open-source tool is purpose-built to kickstart the inventory process, Yadav says. It's a fast, lightweight tool that runs from command line, scans for outward facing TLS and SSH services, and creates an inventory for the IP range it's pointed at.

"You start with nothing but a domain name and by the end you get a complete cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM)," Yadav says. The CBOM is an inventory of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols in use, and the scanner pairs it with two scores, one for overall security health and one for post-quantum readiness based on NIST's post-quantum standards.

It also doubles as an outside check on HNDL exposure. Every encrypted session starts with a key exchange, where the two sides agree on a secret. If a public-facing endpoint still uses a classical exchange, traffic an attacker records today could be unlocked later by a quantum computer. A hybrid exchange that adds post-quantum math protects that traffic, provided the client uses it too, and the scanner reports which kind each endpoint offers.

Classical endpoints are the ones most exposed to HNDL, and Yadav sees AC Scanner as giving organizations a starting point for making HNDL-aware transition plans.

Of course, any security professional will be quick to point out that a scan is just an informational snapshot. It's what happens after that information is in hand that really counts. Scanning tools can kickstart discovery, but organizations need to follow up what they find with a migration plan and start executing on it. NIST’s Regenscheid says the sooner organizations can get to these plans, the better.

"Given how long these transitions take, the organizations that start planning and begin moving to post-quantum products and services now will be in a far stronger position later," he says, stating that this is an opportunity to modernize a lot of the process. "Many steps must occur in sequence, which is why an early start is crucial."

From a security point of view, was fetching an unused dependency a potential attack vector? (like changing global state even without calling exported functions or using global data).

I don't know Rust enough to be sure but I don't think so. It only affect the package manager and not the compiler.

There is a risk in Cargo from unused dependencies - Cargo has a build graph based on the declared dependencies in Cargo.toml, and chooses what build steps to run based on that graph. One thing a crate can contain is a build script - which is code that's built and run on the build host at the time of compilation, and can do anything that code running as part of the build system can do.

In theory, an unused dependency can contain a build.rs that's got a security-relevant bug in it; that would then cause a security issue on the build host if you built the unused dependency. Removing it means that's not a problem :-)

First and most important: Safety is cultural. Rust's safety culture uses Rust's safety technology to deliver safety, but you can't just apply that technology and magically get safety, you need the culture. You're damn sure not getting the culture from C. I was a C programmer for decades. Secondly and maybe more understandably to people focused on technology, ALL of Rust follows the same rules and those rules achieve safety. What's different about Safe Rust is that the compiler can check everything you have done in Safe Rust follows the rules, so in Safe Rust following the rules isn't your problem, the compiler will check that. The "safe subset" technology can't work without a language where everybody else is following the safety rules all the time. So leaving aside the harder culture problem, step one is to have safety rules for C and get everybody to follow them all the time. This is extremely hard - I believe impossible - but it's a pre-requisite, you can't start with the safe subset.

For me Rust is more a successor to C++, but less so for C.

The C language has a small core language, while both C++ and Rust have a larger set of core features (so without taking into account the standard library).

I use the C language in combination with GLib/GObject, where all symbols need to be used with their fully qualified names. For instance when reading a gtk_widget_set_visible() function call, you know that it comes from the GTK library (the namespace), from the GtkWidget class and it's the set_visible() method. A fully-qualified name improves the comprehension when reading the code. (Code is read more often than written, so it's useful to ease code understandability; also for reviewing patches).

Type inference: I prefer explicit/manifest typing for all variables. It also improves code reasoning IMHO. Same problem for code review tools that may lack some features present in the text editor or IDE to show type information when hovering the mouse on a variable name.

The shadowing feature for variables looks to me a bad practice. It should be: one variable name, one usage. So something like

The .. operator versus ..= (creating half-open and closed ranges, respectively). Off-by-one errors are so frequent in programming that such succinct syntax can be misleading when reading quickly some piece of code. Example:

It doesn't follow the more standard mathematics notation:

At some point, in programming languages a more classic for loop with an integer variable is clearer:

Succinct code creates more logic errors IMHO. Even though Rust is much safer with the compiler, I suspect there will be more such kind of logic bugs. Code obfuscation and backdoors are perhaps trickier to detect with such subtle operators.

BTW, the "fn" keyword is not really fun in some countries (political parties).

The lack of a semicolon which means that it's the return value looks also something weird and subtle to catch for the eyes. I prefer an explicit return keyword.

Natural languages have many redundancies (plural forms in a sentence, e.g.). When reading or listening, a small inattention is not a problem because you can catch up thanks to the redundancies.

That was also my opinion when I started programming in Rust. But soon I realized that the return is just redundant and it's actually much easier to read without it. A function always returns something. Even if it's (). Why write `return` then? The last thing is always returned. Rust actually is much more consistent than C and C++ here, where void is kind of a special case. All of the other things you said: You can just do as you wish. Rust doesn't prevent you from adding a return statement to the end of the function. Or adding types to all local variables. Or using full path syntax all over the place, or just use plain C-style function names all over the place, etc. Except for the for-loop thing everything can be done, if you like it better. The for-loop thing can probably easily be implemented with a macro.

Fully-qualified function call syntax is possible to use everywhere, again modulo unnameable types, but it looks quite ugly. While I agree that (for example) foo.into() is a bit ambiguous about what conversion we're performing, you can fix that by writing Bar::from(foo) if you prefer. Nobody in their right mind is going to write >::into(foo) or >::from(foo). (Those latter syntaxes exist to disambiguate the case where multiple traits define from() or into() methods or associated functions, or where Foo and Bar have inherent implementations of those methods or associated functions. But From and Into are well-known stdlib traits, so such a collision is unlikely in practice. It would be more plausible with more obscure traits, and fully qualified syntax is commonly used in macros because you can't know ahead of time that a collision is impossible.)

shadow_reuse lints cases where you re-use the value, for example maybe "width" on line 10 doesn't including padding but "width" on line 20 onwards adds 10 for padding. shadow_same lints cases where the shadow is just fiddling with the mutability or references, so maybe "goose" on line 10 is an actual Goose, but on line 20 onwards it's now just a mutable reference to the same goose. shadow_unrelated lints almost the opposite case from shadow_reuse, maybe "depth" on line 10 is an integer number of pixels while on line 20 onwards it's a 3D buffer. It might seem as though, since Rust has lints for so many misuses of shadowing, the whole idea of shadowing comes into disrepute, but in fact the argument for shadowing is that it is more readable - when done appropriately. Some codebases where shadowing is forbidden have to work around this. In languages like Rust with a good static type system this can encourage use of weaker, rubbish types and mutability when you'd be better off with immutable strong types and some shadowing. let delay : bool = /* somehow we discover a bool --- yes or no we want a delay here */ let delay : Duration = /* we make a (perhaps zero) Duration -- representing some amount of time */ let delay : MyHTMLType = /* some HTML about that delay */ If you forbid shadowing, you tempt somebody to decide booleans, durations and pointers to some HTML are all just basically integers, so we can say this is an integer and make it mutable then re-assign it, changing what it means repeatedly but sneaking past our "no shadowing" rule. Alternatively maybe they name these variables delay_bool, delay_duration and delay_html but we already HAVE a type system, why are you shovelling this into variable names?

#9833. A NES emulator written in Odin

I’ve started this project in late June of 2024. I’ve worked on it in my spare time off and on. I decided to put a pause on this project in January 2025 to focus on other things.

It’s been a wild ride. I’ve had a lot of fun, but I’ve also suffered more towards the end, when trying to make the emulator “fully” accurate.

You can read the Github Readme for more info about the project.

I’ve seen some people say that making a NES emulator is a simple weekend project, and I frankly found that baffling. Because evidently, it’s not. It took me 7 months to get my emulator to how it is now.

I think what they actually mean is that getting a NES emulator “working” takes a short time. Like maybe getting Donkey Kong to run. And that’s true. You can get to 80% or maybe 90% pretty fast. It’s the last 10% that takes a long, long time.

The NES hardware has many idiosyncrasies that need to be emulated for certain games to run. Many games depend on very specific NES behavior. And if you don’t implement it right, they won’t run. A lot of the challenge is about timing. The CPU and the PPU (the chip that handles the graphics rendering in the NES) run in parallel and they communicate with each other. That timing needs to be very accurate, or many wrong things can happen. Most games will run fine with a less than accurate emulator, but a lot of them won’t, and they will need you to consider things in more detail.

Another issue is mappers. Mappers are what we call an implementation of a type of cartridge. You see, NES games come in cartridges, and cartridges aren’t just data. They are circuitry with their own behavior and extra resources like read-only memory, and writable memory. Some come with extra audio capabilities, but I haven’t implemented that.

Anyway, you have to implement these mappers if you want a game that comes in that cartridge to run in your game. They complete the NES’s circuitry. In a way, they are a part of the NES hardware. There are many mappers, but you can support a lot of games by just implementing a few. I’ve had trouble implementing some mappers, and some of them are still badly implemented, causing some games to not work. I found it hard to understand some of the mapper documentation.

The biggest challenge with making an emulator, I think, is to know what to implement. Information about the hardware, and what needs to be emulated about the hardware for games to work in your emulator. Thankfully, the NES is very well documented online. I’ve used many resources, like:

I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without these resources and the help from people in the nesdev discord.

I’ve learned a lot about Odin while making this project. I think it fit this project like a glove. Being a very simple, strongly typed C-like language that gives me all the freedom I want makes making an emulator much easier than using other languages, I feel.

One thing that threw me off was that Odin has no automatic integer promotion. When doing calculations on numbers, Odin will never promote types to a bigger one. That led to a few bugs. But I blame this all on me and me being used to C’s integer promotion.

One fun thing that I’ve learned was doing a bit of memory allocation strategy. Odin has no automatic memory management, so you have to come up with smart ways to handle memory. I’ve had fun thinking about how I should handle memory best. I didn’t need to do anything complicated. I mostly use one temporary allocator that clears every frame, a global heap allocator for things that need to live forever, and a NES Arena allocator for anything that needs to live along a NES session. I found memory allocation fun.

Another thing I had to learn is how to serialize Odin objects. I used the CBOR library, and I ran into a few issues. I thought my code was misbehaving due to a bug in the library, but that was cleared up. It was only having trouble because I made a few odd types that it didn’t know how to serialize. Once I learned how to properly write custom handling for types, everything worked perfectly. This was one of the tricky types that cbor didn’t know how to serialize:

I love how Odin lets you define raw unions like this, and with bit fields. It fits emulator development very well.

I don’t consider this project “finished”. Of course, a project like this is never truly finished, but a lot of aspects of it need a lot of work, for sure:

#9832. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Doing The Right Thing: Accountability In The Age Of AI Coding Summary

In this podcast, Shane Hastie, Lead Editor for Culture & Methods, spoke to Hugo Venturini about who is accountable when AI writes the code, how AI is reshaping code review and traditional engineering roles, and how leaders build a culture of transparency and psychological safety.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Shane Hastie: Good day, folks. This is Shane Hastie for the InfoQ Engineering Culture Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Hugo Venturini. Hugo, welcome. Thank you for taking the time to talk to us.

Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me.

Shane Hastie: Now, we are sitting in opposite sides of the world. I'm in New Zealand and you are somewhere in Europe.

Hugo Venturini: Yes, right now I'm in Spain, in Valencia.

Shane Hastie: Nice. You've got a beautiful warm summer. I'm sitting in a pretty cold winter, but we'll get past that. My normal starting point with these conversations is, who's Hugo?

Hugo Venturini: So I'm a software engineer. I defended my PhD on the debugging of optimized code in 2008. And after that, I joined the industry as a software engineer and I climbed the ladder one step after the other. Senior then manager. I was a manager at Meta, Facebook at the time. I was accountable for the type checker and the compiler of the hack language. Eventually I decided to try to create my own company, grew it, then joined another organization, was the CTO of Qwant, the search engine, 90 people in the organization from network engineers to AI researchers. And right now, I work in a software company, startup company that deals with tooling for AI, to help AI do the right thing, so to speak.

Shane Hastie: The right thing. What do we mean when we say, "The right thing", today?

Hugo Venturini: Somebody's making a decision about what should be provided as a product to users. Somebody's about to write the code. Somebody will test it. Somebody will make the decision to release this to prod and somebody will use it. It can be all different people or it can be the same person at every step. Doing the right thing, to me, is solving the problem to a user. And then at every step, you got doing the right thing of that step. And for a code generation, it is generating the proper code to some extent.

Shane Hastie: Now, somebody made a decision, but all too often today we are seeing the addiction of, "Yeah, but the agent did this. The code generator did this".

Hugo Venturini: I think humans are in charge and humans should be accountable and are, most of the time, at least to what I can see, and that's the right thing. I'm not minimizing what it does, but AI is just another tool. It's a very powerful tool. And don't get me wrong, I still got these wow moments several times, not a day, but at least a week. And yet if it fails, the one conducting this great tool is accountable, is in charge and should answer what goes wrong. Doing the proper thing is doing what the human asks it to do. And when you want to generate code, code has to be to the colon, to the semi-colon, to the character. And if it does not, many times, the proper tooling can actually tell the AI how to loop and give the right feedback. So when it comes back to the human, a great deal of what could be automated has been automated.

Shane Hastie: One of the things that we are seeing, and various studies are pointing to this, the size of pull requests are getting bigger and bigger. I've heard stories of the 2000 lines, a senior engineer who's got a backlog of over 300 pull requests, each of which is hundreds of lines long waiting to be reviewed.

Hugo Venturini: First, the size of pull request is a problem which does not rise with AI. It was already existing before. And the first thing is asking yourself, "Should I review everything?" Sometimes you got all that boilerplate. We could already, before AI, automate the verification. Let me do this. If it compiles, that's already a good thing. If it passes all the tests you've created, if it behaves the way you wanted it, do you really need to review the code? That was already not the case before.

Second thing is, already before as well, and I've lived in an organization that was working like this, you don't have to go for a signature of a diff for every single diff you do. Eventually people are good enough, senior enough or do trust each other that says, "I can totally merge this diff without having anybody reviewed it. And if it goes wrong, I'm accountable for fixing it. That'd be okay, but I'm totally sure and people trust me to merge it already". And sometimes you've got the heart of the product which you want to create and you need to be able to review for two reasons. First, for quality. Second, for sharing the knowledge, of course. And sometimes it's really just boilerplate that you can totally merge it.

With AI, big reviews always, and you can still, I believe, not go for who's got the biggest review, but who's handy enough to get your AI to create the proper diff and the proper stack of diff. So you get only one to review what the heart of the product is. I think with AI, because of the wow effect, some people are playing this game of the wow effect with, "Look, I have rewritten this entire big product in only one diff", which is just for the show. Let's face it, nobody does this. And before, at the group of engineers, if anybody were doing this, we were all telling him or her, "Please, help us review your code". That's one thing. And after that, you got the number of diffs and that's another problem.

How do you review for number of diffs? I don't have any good answer and I'm really eager to have anybody telling me, "How do you do this?" Right now, what we've decided in my team is we don't review everything. We were not reviewing everything before and we trust people with our own good judgments that this needs not being reviewed and we only ask proactively, "This, I want you to review it". I give you two other reasons for that. And this, I can merge it already. And so this minimize number of diffs to be reviewed by other people. But that's an open conversation I'm sure we all want to have, like, "How do others do about this?" And please, tell me.

Shane Hastie: We'll leave that as an open question for the audience to respond. So what are the implications of this in terms of the broader elements of quality in our product? And we think of the architectural frameworks and so forth, how do we make sure that we are building the right stuff?

Hugo Venturini: I got a story about rising quality in an unexpected way, at least for some. I worked with Microsoft in 2014 when they decided to merge the software engineer branch with the testers branch. At the time, testers were doing two things. Some were not coding, some were coding, and the software engineers were writing software and handing it to the testers for testing and was going back and forth. By removing the official testing step by somebody else, it actually raised the quality of the software. And the reason I believe is because it made software engineers accountable for the final product, not one step of the chain.

Today, I got the feeling that we are removing the software and everybody's becoming a tester via your AI, because you command some software which is written and then people become software. But we are all, again, merging those two verticals as one. And the difference is, we don't see an increase of quality yet, and I believe it's because people are still blaming the AI and don't feel accountable for what the tooling is doing. And that's one thing we totally need to work on as leaders, as managers, as colleagues, as users. I've seen some software I've been using definitely lacking quality over the last month. And I read in the press that those people are massively using AI and I'm like, "Maybe I see something here". And I'd like to know what kind of feedback I can give to get them back on quality.

Shane Hastie: So with collapsing roles, so you mentioned the engineer, the tester. What about the architect? What about the product manager? What about the security tester, the compliance elements?

Hugo Venturini: The more people you have in an org, the more narrowed focus you have for people. When you're in a startup company, you are everybody. The tester, the PM, the architect, and sometimes the users, the dogfooter and the HR and the finance, you're everybody. And the bigger the org grows and the more people you need in every single verticals, and eventually you have a PM for the front end, a technical PM for the backend. You're going to have a handful of software engineer for the front, from the back, for the queues, and the more it grows and then it becomes like an army of people working on it. And with AI, we try to shrink it back again to when the industry was growing, to when the company was growing and we face sometimes some misunderstanding of people who have never been a PM, even a bad PM, but when you have to be a PM because you're a startup company, you eventually do the job.

And when the AI comes, it really helps you. When you've never been, but you can be and you're asked to be, that's something you have to learn. I believe that we need some more trainings or help for all those people because AI really, really empowers you, but it empowers you to do things that you're not sure how to do, and that's where AI barely helps you. It always answers the question you're asking, but if you're asking the wrong questions and being a senior is asking the right questions, the good question that helps grow, that helps define, that's being a senior. Senior is, with experience and knowledge, you actually ask the question that helps move forward to a solution. And I believe we need to help people being better at asking the right questions to the AI, if you really want it to succeed.

Shane Hastie: It worries me that the software engineer who's being used to being asked to build this and given some sort of a spec, whether it's a set of user stories, a screen mock-up or just a quick conversation, we're now asking that person to think of the right questions to ask. What is the implication of that? We've spoken about shift left and shift right for the last couple of decades. We're shifting further left, but have we and how do we empower and give the people who are being now asked to do the questioning to do that left shift to know how to do that work?

Hugo Venturini: People dare to do things if they know they will be accountable but not blamed for what happens. And that's an organization, that's a human part of your organization. If you empower people, but they don't dare, you're just not doing anything. And that comes back to the human, to managers, to organizations. How do you empower your people and give them not only the tooling, but also the state of mind of stepping out of your comfort zone? I'm a software engineer and as I said, I have to also explore a broader space. What if I don't dare? What if I can't? Because even though I got all the tooling I have, I fear it. I fear the organization I work with. And that's something which is... This is a hard part. I mean, human is the hard part of the software industry, right?

Shane Hastie: So this is culture. This is the Engineering Culture Podcast. How do I nurture that culture?

Hugo Venturini: I'm not sure that the recipe... Sorry, I know there's no recipe. However, I got some good examples where I believe it was the right move. The first thing is transparency and honesty. If you are honest with your team, most of the time people start being honest. I eventually became the CTO of a company which had a broken culture. People would lie, hide, steal, everything was wrong. And I was asked to fix the culture, so to speak. And very quickly I decided to lead by example. So I started to have a Q&A every week. You can ask me any question. If I can answer, I answer. If I can't, you have to keep me accountable for answering the next time. And you ask me the question again, and if I don't answer, ask it again until you have the answer. No judgment about it. Of course, first Q&A, I only got easy questions.

People wouldn't dare to challenge the head of the org. And I started to come with answers such as, "I don't know. I made a mistake. This is a good thing. Congratulations, but you don't name people. You only name solutions and product. You are accountable for what you're doing and you take the load whenever. And coming back with the last time you asked me these questions and I found the answer and it is unpleasant, but you need to hear it and we are all in this together and gathering the thing". Eventually after a few sessions, people started to ask me difficult questions and eventually we started to go with even more difficult questions by allowing for an anonymous board. So I asked my managers, "What about you ask them if they have questions and if they have it on there, write it down and you ask it. Even better, you give it to another manager so I cannot even guess which team it comes from, but I want the questions. I don't care who ask it, so please dare".

And they started to organize this so I could never guess from which part of the organization the question was coming, but I got the questions and eventually people started to vote for questions and it grew like this and it becomes very interesting. Eventually people would stack questions before the Q&A. What I noticed in the org is, when I arrived, people would lie to me and I would see it. And I was like, "Okay, you can totally confront the person, 'You're lying to me, that's bad.'" I said, "No, no, no. It's a cultural thing. How do I take it as a whole and shift almost the entire culture of lying, of hiding things by being transparent and explaining things and showing them that I can be accountable and move forward and fix things?" Being exemplary is when you can totally break things as long as you've fixed them before and you learn a lesson and you don't repeat your mistakes.

Being wrong and making mistakes is totally acceptable. What is not acceptable is repeating your own mistakes because you have not learned, so you have not grown. And this cultural thing of allowing people totally shift the essence of this organization, which went much better by the time, but you also have to be patient. When you write software, you see it right away under your hands, maybe a few hours later. With humans, you need to learn patience, but eventually you see results.

Shane Hastie: Beautiful story and a great example of shifting culture. What if I'm not high enough up in the organization to do this?

Hugo Venturini: Okay. First, there's nothing as just a team lead. You are a team lead. That's not just a team lead. And at every level you got something to contribute to and to help grow. I've seen it work in smaller teams. Eventually I was in a startup company, a startup. We were already at 1200 in the company, so it was scale up, you say. And I found two teams were already working like this at their level. They were already working on this transparency and we are a team, but also we also need to be accountable. And I've seen it work. It was less efficient in terms of, I would say, impact because it was at the size of the one team and not the entire org, but already very interesting. And the good thing is, managers also gather together. I mean, as a manager, you have a team, but you are part of another team which is a team of managers.

And that's the difficulty of being a manager that most people don't get. First is, you're not only manager of a team, you are now a member of two teams with sometimes different goals or opposite goals. As a manager, you need to think outside of your own team to help the org at the size of every manager. As a manager of a team, you need to help the team grow and sometimes you have to make decisions that won't please either the rest of the managers or sometimes your team, and it cannot only be one way. You have to think outside of your own team to make it grow and make it better. And that's maybe the most difficult part of being a manager. And at every level, you always have a way to influence right outside. If you start to do the right thing and you actually see benefits, you can talk about it to other managers and eventually they will follow you and do the same thing and eventually it will grow. Okay, this is wishful thinking maybe, but if you don't try, you know it won't work, right?

Shane Hastie: Yeah. If you don't even try, you're guaranteed to fail.

Hugo Venturini: The way I see it is, as a manager, I'm here to help people. So I would always, not maybe always phrase it this way, but I'd say, "Help me help you". So if you provide the right information to your manager, your manager would be able to help you. If you hide too much, if you're too secret on some part of who you are or what you do, it becomes a little harder. You're not only a machine coding or being an engineer, you're also a human. And sometimes you got ups and downs and if you provide some information to help your manager, your manager can also totally help you. And that works at every level.

As a CTO, I was at the COMEX and talking with the CEO, the CFO, and if you give them some hints that they can help you because you are in a down moment or hub moment or you are available to help them, you become a member of the team. And it's not a day by day. It's an average, it's going to be 50/50 in the end, but it doesn't have to be you always being 50% helped and being helpful every day by the hour, by the week, it's overall. But it's kind of hard thing because you don't know when it ends.

Shane Hastie: We are dealing with people.

Hugo Venturini: I like to help people. I like to see people grow. Most of the time, staff relationship in helping people, and that's all why I moved to the management and leadership roles because I believe that most of people are better than I am at what they do in their job. So if I can help them be even better, it cascades to the next person and the overall organization grows.

Shane Hastie: So the manager as amplifier.

And that's also why when you got toxic management, it's devastating for an org. The impact is easier when you got people reporting to you, but also as easier, it's easier to destroy everything or to grow better.

Shane Hastie: We've handed a lot and given some good advice around that transparency and bringing that into culture and the culture of accountability without blame. What is the really important question that I haven't asked you?

Hugo Venturini: We've talked about management and the impact that come with the role. Is it possible to have the same kind of impact without being a manager? I've seen individuals being able to do this, and I've been always very much impressed by their level of influence, and I'm not sure I've deciphered how they were working. What I've seen is, those people were technically very strong, very humble, and the common characteristic of those people were like, they were always, always listening more than they were speaking. So yes, it is possible, but I'm also leaning towards the conclusion that it's not everybody is able to do it. There's something natural in those people, and when you ask them, they're like, "I don't know. I got it by chance. For some reason people are listening to me". I'm like, "Oh, come on, dude. You know that's wrong. You work on your skills, but also you've met the right people". Everybody's been mentored. Nobody came naturally to this kind of position.

Hugo Venturini: That's the one thing is, you can totally grow. It is possible, and it can be a north star to have this kind of influence. And if you don't reach this kind of influence, maybe you're too humble to understand that you are actually at this level of influence, and it is more probable that it's your humility that forgives you to see it than the fact that you are not at this level of influence. But yes, it is possible. It is a very tough career. Some of the best leaders I've met as ICs, many, many of them tried being manager for a while and came back. And the easiest and best seniors, staff, principal engineers I've managed knew the role of managers and knew how to help me as a manager.

So I would say give it a go. It doesn't have to last for your life. I mean, you can totally give it a try for a moment. I was an IC at Microsoft, became a manager, was hired as an IC at Facebook, became a manager, eventually created my company, was an IC, then became a manager, and then was hired as director, a CTO. I've been an IC for a bit more than a year. Going back and forth gives you all the understanding of the scope of what is it to create the product that answers a user's demand. In the end, it's just about this, I believe.

Shane Hastie: That pendulum swing across roles. You got a lot of really interesting and meaty stuff there. If people want to continue the conversation, where can they find you?

Hugo Venturini: They can find me on X/XTwitter as monsieurv. It’s French. My alias is monsieurv. And on LinkedIn, by my name, Hugo Venturini. Please, please come and discuss it all. You agree, you disagree, you have another story, you have questions, you have things to raise questions from me, because I'm very curious. Please keep this conversation going. I think it's a fascinating space, and we decided to be in this space because it is fascinating because the meeting of software and humans is an ongoing conversation that's going to be for life.

Shane Hastie: Hugo, thanks so much for taking the time.

Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me in your podcast. Very, very interesting conversation.

#9830. cursor:pointer on buttons

Three weeks ago, at a CSS Working Grouping meeting, we discussed an issue “Cursors for base appearance”, and resolved on the following:

The CSS Working Group just discussed [css-forms-1] Cursors for base appearance, and agreed to the following:

One of the rules from the “last comment” mentioned there is

Or, if we were to remove all non-button selectors,

That is, of course, not a change to the default styles in the browser — this is a rule for elements that will have an appearance: base-….

Also note that, this user agent style will be very much overrideable — no !important.

Anyone who does not like cursor: pointer on buttons and other similar elements, are free to override it to default (or anything else) in their stylesheets.

The rest of us can, I guess, celebrate? I was always on the side of this decision. I published my “Correct Cursor on Active Elements” article in 2013. In 2017, I opened my first CSSWG issue — “Change the pointer cursor to indicate any interactive element”, which led to a change in a non-normative part of the spec.

Since then, I did not see any new arguments in this debate. I will not repeat everything that I argued about, but one of the most common counter-arguments that I read today is “OS does not do it”.

Did you see that “OS”? When was the last time your OS innovated anything in the UI? Did it become easier to use over years?

Many of people with this argument ask, thinking that this will be a good question, something like “What next — change the cursor in the OS?!”.

I mean… Yes? I would be happy with that. When I look at like half of the (non-native) apps in my desktop OS, they have cursor: pointer on interactive elements.

Cinny, Discord, Signal, Slack, Steam, VS Code — some of the apps that I have before me.

When I use apps that do not change the cursor to anything other than default, I cringe.

Default cursor does not communicate anything. It does one job well — point at a specific pixel. It could do more.

In the issue, many people came with dislikes and their arguments against cursor: pointer. I want to aknowledge one argument that I fully agree with — it would be great if buttons and links would have different cursors. And also, regular links should have cursors different from the links that are opened in new tabs.

But if we were to look at those three things:

And then had only two cursors to assign to all of them, I know which ones I will assign to which.

And I will never understand anyone thinking that buttons have more in common with blank space than with links.

#9829. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗

Compare two TTS voices and pick the more natural one

Explore ASR model benchmarks across datasets and languages

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS."

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard
