#9820. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures

Nov 13, 2026 2 min read

Google has open-sourced AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns, and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses.

AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging, or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters, and tracking issues. Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics. AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment, or on demand.

For root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment. Its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges, and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs, or retrieved data. AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically.

AQuA sidecar architecture (Source: Google Developer Blog Post)

Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters. The verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation.

After developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero, and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13. These results came from controlled replay, not production traffic.

An insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score.

Findings link to supporting traces, and proposed root causes must reference valid lines in the deployed snapshot. AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING, or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed. Sampling can miss rare failures, and replay may not reproduce external state.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn, Dmytro Aprelenko, engineering manager at Redcore, wrote,

Agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early.

AQuA validates source references and links findings to supporting traces. Cluster verification filters false positives, though it cannot confirm every session exhibits the same failure. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code.

Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. Its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows.

#9817. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

InfoQ Homepage News Siri AI Developer Preview Lets iOS, iPadOS, and macOS Apps Integrate with Siri

Nov 13, 2026 2 min read

Apple released the Siri AI Developer Preview in the 27.3 beta releases of its operating systems, enabling developers and apps to integrate with the assistant and hand off actions to it. During the Preview, access to Siri AI is restricted to developer builds and internal TestFlight testers.

Apple says that Siri AI is an entirely new version of its assistant which is "profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal".

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more.

These new capabilities let users make natural language requests and have Siri AI carry out any custom action supported by the app. The framework also supports complex requests through Skills, a new feature that lets developers "teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience".

If a request does not specify an app name, it will automatically be routed to the app currently in the foreground, the app associated with an active Live Activity, or the app previously mentioned in the ongoing conversation. This allows users to continue conversations across an app and its Live Activity, or a different app altogether. While an app is running in the background, however, it will receive only requests that explicitly mention its name.

Requests can also include actions across apps, such as finding content in one app, sending it to another, and performing an action there.

Commenting on Apple's announcement, Reddit user sixtypercenttogether noted:

In my limited testing so far it does what it says. If you include a good description on your intent and parameters, Siri can figure it out. THIS is what Siri should have been all along, all the way back in 26.0.

User Medical_Lengthiness6 compared Apple's approach to integrating Siri AI to Google's AppFunctions:

Doing it via app intents was the right move. Google could have done this with the android intents but instead decided to make a completely different agent skills sdk that you have to implement.

All Apple Intelligence features, including Siri AI, may be subject to usage limits, with extended, premium access planned for the future. Finally, developers based in the EU should be aware that Siri AI is currently unavailable in the EU on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9815. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9814. Shadow AI in the Workplace: Data Security Risks and Governance Strategies

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

3rd-year law student writing on Generative AI, Intellectual Property policy, and the impact of technology on human cognition.

A junior associate is sitting at their desk, trying to finish a 110-page agreement that has to be ready by 8:00 AM. The coffee has gone cold. After hours of reading the same pages, even simple clauses are becoming difficult to understand.

There is still a lot of work left, and very little time.

The associate opens a free AI chatbot on a personal phone and copies three clauses from the agreement. Within seconds, the tool provides a short summary. The work becomes a little easier, and the associate moves on to the next task.

But there is one problem. The law firm has already banned the use of public AI tools. Its computers block access to these websites, and employees have been warned not to use them for professional work. Yet the associate has found another way to access the same tool through a personal device.

The firm's system may show that its restrictions are working. But it cannot necessarily show what the associate has shared through a personal connection.

This is one way Shadow AI can enter a workplace. The employee may not intend to expose confidential information. They may simply be trying to finish an urgent task. But the information has still moved outside the organisation's control. And this raises a question that companies need to consider: If employees are still finding ways to use AI despite a workplace ban, is blocking access really enough to protect the organisation?

Shadow AI refers to the use of artificial intelligence tools by employees without the knowledge or approval of their organisation. These tools may include public chatbots, AI writing assistants, browser extensions, coding tools and meeting transcription applications.

The problem is not limited to which tool an employee uses. It is also about what information they share with it.

An employee may upload a client document to get a summary, enter company data to prepare a report, or share a section of source code to find an error. These actions may appear harmless from the employee's point of view. However, the organisation may have no clear understanding of where that information goes, how it is stored or what happens to it after the task is completed.

Many companies have responded by restricting or blocking public AI platforms. Their concerns are understandable. Confidential information, customer records and business documents should not be shared with services that have not been properly assessed.

However, a restriction does not automatically change employee behaviour. If a company blocks an AI website but continues to expect employees to complete the same workload within the same deadlines, the reason for using AI does not disappear. Some employees may simply find another way to access it.

This is where the real problem begins. A company may successfully block an application on its office network while remaining unaware that employees are using the same application through personal phones, private accounts or other connections.

Banning AI may restrict access through official systems, but it does not necessarily stop its use. In some situations, it can move that use beyond the organisation's visibility.

The use of AI at work is growing faster than many organisations can introduce their own systems and policies.

Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index reported that 75% of global knowledge workers were using AI at work. Among those using AI, 78% were bringing their own AI tools to work, commonly described as Bring Your Own AI (BYOAI).

This pattern aligns with broader enterprise trends. Research from Gartner shows that over 41% of employees actively acquire, modify, or use technology outside the visibility of IT department.

These figures are important because they show that employees are not waiting for their organisations to introduce every tool they want to use. But they should be understood carefully: they show workplace AI adoption and the use of personal tools; they do not prove that corporate bans are the reason employees use them.

The reasons can be practical. A legal associate may want to understand a long agreement more quickly. A researcher may need to organise a large amount of information. A software engineer may want help finding an error in code. An employee preparing a presentation may use AI to create an initial draft.

In each case, the employee is trying to save time or complete a task more efficiently.

This does not make every use acceptable. Employees still have a responsibility to follow workplace policies and protect confidential information. But organisations also need to understand why employees are turning to tools that have not been approved.

A policy that only says "do not use AI" may not answer the questions employees face every day: Which tools can I use? What information can I share? What should I do when the approved system cannot handle my task?

When these questions remain unanswered, employees may make their own decisions. That is how a technology policy can become disconnected from actual workplace behaviour.

In April 2023, Samsung Electronics reportedly faced incidents in which employees entered sensitive internal information into ChatGPT. Reports described employees sharing semiconductor source code and internal meeting information while using the tool for work-related tasks.

The incident became an important warning for companies considering the use of public AI platforms. It showed that sensitive information can leave an organisation through an ordinary workplace activity. An employee does not need to hack a system or deliberately attack a company. Copying information into an external chatbot can itself create a serious exposure.

Samsung's response included restrictions on generative AI use. The incident demonstrates why companies became concerned about employees using public AI tools. It does not, by itself, prove that bans push employees towards personal devices. That is a separate issue that organisations need to examine through evidence about employee behaviour.

There is another important point here. When information is entered into an external AI service, the organisation needs to understand the service's data practices.

Different AI providers have different terms and settings. Some services may use submitted content for model improvement under certain conditions, while others offer business arrangements with different data-retention and training terms. It would be incorrect to assume that every public AI service handles every prompt in the same way.

The concern is that employees using personal accounts may not know which terms apply to their information. The organisation may also have no contract, security review or clear process through which it can manage that risk.

For companies and legal institutions, Shadow AI is not just an IT concern. It can affect confidential information, legal responsibilities, customer trust and business interests.

1.⁠ ⁠Confidentiality and Attorney-Client Privilege

Legal professionals regularly work with sensitive information. This includes client communications, draft agreements, litigation strategies, personal records and documents that have not been made public.

Uploading such material to an external AI service without proper approval can create serious confidentiality concerns.

However, it is important to distinguish confidentiality from attorney-client privilege. Sharing privileged information with a third-party service does not automatically waive privilege in every situation. The legal result depends on the jurisdiction, the circumstances of disclosure, the service provider's access and the steps taken to maintain confidentiality.

Even where privilege is not automatically lost, sharing client information without proper safeguards may raise professional, contractual or ethical concerns.

For a law firm, the question should therefore not be limited to whether an AI tool gives a useful answer. It should also ask whether the information being shared is permitted to leave the firm's controlled environment.

2.⁠ ⁠Data Protection and Financial Penalties

The risk becomes more serious when employees share personal information through unapproved AI tools.

For example, a document may contain a client's name, address, financial details, identification information or other personal data. If that information is sent to an external service without appropriate safeguards, the organisation may face data-protection questions.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for penalties for specified failures. Under its Schedule, failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches can attract a penalty of up to ₹250 crore. This does not mean that every employee's use of an AI chatbot automatically leads to that penalty. The relevant legal duties, facts and circumstances must be considered.

Similarly, under the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), certain serious infringements can attract fines of up to €20 million or 4% of the undertaking's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

These figures show why organisations need to take the handling of personal information seriously. But financial penalties are only one part of the problem. A data incident can also affect customer confidence, business relationships and the organisation's reputation.

IBM's 2023 Cost of a Data Breach Report estimated the global average cost of a data breach at $4.45 million. This is a figure from the 2023 report, not a current estimate specifically for Shadow AI incidents. It nevertheless gives an idea of the financial impact that data breaches can have on organisations.

Companies often hold information that gives them an advantage over competitors. It may include source code, product designs, pricing strategies, financial models, customer information or future business plans.

Keeping such information confidential is an important part of protecting trade secrets.

If employees regularly enter this material into public AI tools without checking the provider's terms or the organisation's security arrangements, the company may weaken its ability to show that it took reasonable steps to protect the information.

The legal position will depend on the relevant law and circumstances. But the business concern is simple: information that was meant to remain inside the organisation may be shared with an external service without proper control.

Blocking AI websites may appear to be the easiest response. A company can restrict access through its network, issue a policy and warn employees against using unapproved tools.

But consider the earlier example of the junior associate. Blocking a website on a company laptop does not prevent the associate from opening the same website on a personal phone. A personal hotspot can also take the activity outside the company's network.

The organisation may see that its office systems are following the policy. It may not see what is happening elsewhere.

This creates a difference between controlling access and controlling actual use.

A company that provides approved AI tools can set rules about who can use them, what information can be shared and which security measures apply. It can also review usage through appropriate technical controls.

By contrast, when employees use personal accounts and devices, the organisation may lose access to important information about that activity. It may not know which tools are being used, what information has been shared or whether an incident has taken place.

This does not mean companies should allow every AI tool. Some uses should remain prohibited, especially where sensitive information cannot be adequately protected. But treating a ban as the complete solution overlooks the reasons employees may continue using AI.

The issue is not simply whether an organisation permits or prohibits AI. It is whether its policy gives employees a safe and practical way to complete their work.

Companies need a system that protects information without ignoring the way employees actually work. This does not require unrestricted AI access. It requires clear rules, suitable tools and safeguards that match the sensitivity of the information.

1.⁠ ⁠Provide Approved Enterprise AI Tools

If employees are using public AI tools because they need help with everyday tasks, organisations should consider providing approved alternatives.

Enterprise AI services may offer different contractual and technical protections, including limits on data retention and commitments about whether customer inputs are used for model training. Some providers also offer Zero Data Retention (ZDR) arrangements.

The aim is to give employees a reliable tool for their daily work without making them depend on personal accounts or unapproved services.

2.⁠ ⁠Use Local AI Models for Highly Sensitive Information

Some work involves information that should not be sent to an external AI service. This may include sensitive source code, confidential legal strategy, certain client documents or important business information.

For such work, organisations can consider running AI models on their own infrastructure or within a controlled private environment.

Open-source model families such as Llama and Mistral may be considered for internal deployment, depending on the organisation's technical needs and resources. For particularly sensitive work, a disconnected or air-gapped system may offer an additional layer of protection.

But local deployment is not automatically safe. The organisation still needs to manage access, system security, updates and the information employees enter into the model.

3.⁠ ⁠Create a Clear Data Classification System

Employees should not have to guess whether a document can be shared with an AI tool. Organisations need to make these rules clear so that employees can understand what information is safe to share and what needs protection.

One practical way to do this is dividing information into three categories: public, internal and condidential.

Public information, such as published reports, press releases, and public case laws, can be used with apporved public or enterprise AI tools. Internal information, including routine meeting notes and general internal dragts, should only be used with AI tools approved under company policy. Confidential information, such as client records, personal data, contracts, source code and M&A information, requries greater care. Employees should use restricted tools or seek additional approval before sharing them.

This system should be easy to understand and connected to the organisation's existing confidentiality rules. Legal teams may need additional restrictions for privileged communications, litigation material and client documents.

Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools can help organisations identify and control the sharing of sensitive information.

For example, these tools can detect personal indentification numbers, financial details or confidential information in data being sent to external AI services. Depending on how the system works, it may block the request, flag it for review or remove senstive information before it reaches an external service.

These tools are not perfect. They may miss information or flag material that is harmless. They should therefore support, rather than replace, clear policies and employee awareness.

Even a well-designed policy can fail if employees do not understand how to follow it in their daily work.

Organisations should explain which AI tools are approved, what information must not be shared, when human review is required and how employees can request access to a new tool.

They should also create a simple way for employees to report accidental disclosure. If people are afraid to report mistakes, organisations may learn about incidents too late to respond effectively.

At the same time, employees must remain responsible for following the rules. Practical alternatives do not remove the duty to protect confidential information. Organisations need both clear expectations and fair accountability.

Shadow AI is not going to disappear simply because an organisation blocks access to certain AI tools. Employees still have deadlines, daily tasks and work to complete. When approved tools are unavailable or difficult to use, some may look for other ways to get the same work done.

This creates a problem for organisations. They may have rules against using unapproved AI services, but those rules do not necessarily tell them where employees are actually using AI or what information they are sharing.

This does not mean employees should be free to use any tool they want. Confidential information still needs protection, and employees must take responsibility for how they use AI. But organisations also need to look at why employees are turning to tools outside the approved system.

If a tool is helping employees complete routine work more easily, the organisation should consider whether it can provide a safe alternative. It should also make clear what information can be shared and where approval is required.

The real issue is not just whether employees are following AI policies. It is whether those policies work in the way people actually do their jobs. If organisations want to manage Shadow AI, they need to understand its use rather than simply try to stop it.

InfoQ Homepage News Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability

Nov 14, 2026 2 min read

DocumentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of the open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL, with compatibility for the MongoDB wire protocol. Most MongoDB drivers, tools, and queries work without changes.

DocumentDB consists of a PostgreSQL extension that provides MongoDB API-compatible functionality and a gateway that translates MongoDB protocol requests into PostgreSQL calls. Version 1.0 supports PostgreSQL 15–18 through container images, with Linux packages available for PostgreSQL 17 and 18, and includes a Kubernetes operator, with the GA focusing on security, stability, and fixes for indexing, aggregation, and geospatial queries.

Microsoft announced the open source project early in 2025, aiming to provide the developer community with a NoSQL datastore built on PostgreSQL, and offering full visibility into the engine's architecture and implementation. The project joined the Linux Foundation a few months later, with support from other large database organizations including AWS, Cockroach Labs, Google, Snowflake, and Yugabyte. In the recent article "DocumentDB and the MIT License: What to Know Before You Build, Deploy, and Distribute," the team explains how DocumentDB’s permissive MIT license allows commercial use, modification, and hosting without requiring disclosure of proprietary code, contrasting it with MongoDB’s SSPL.

Even if the project provides a page discussing the DocumentDB name disambiguation, covering the open source project, Azure DocumentDB, and Azure Cosmos DB, the community remains perplexed about the choice. In a popular Hacker News thread, user marifjeren writes:

Name it anything else for god's sake. DocumentDB is already what everybody calls Amazon DocumentDB.

With multiple open source options now on the market, Patty Chow, product manager at Microsoft, explains why open-source document databases need multiple implementations to give developers more choice in deployment and infrastructure while preserving compatibility with MongoDB drivers and queries. Chow writes:

MongoDB has given developers a widely used way to work with document data. Familiar drivers and query patterns are worth preserving. Alternative implementations give developers a chance to keep using that knowledge while evaluating different approaches to storage and deployment.

In a Reddit thread, some practitioners raise concerns about current MongoDB compatibility and confusion with similarly named products. User 716green comments:

Compatibility between MongoDB and FerretDB has been absolutely minimal compared to what you would probably expect. I've been a fan of DocumentDB for a long time and I love that Microsoft is supporting FerretDB.

DocumentDB provides the PostgreSQL extensions and its own MongoDB-compatible gateway, while FerretDB is a separate project that uses the DocumentDB extensions as its backend and provides its own MongoDB-compatible interface.

Layerbase recently ran an initial comparison of FerretDB and the PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB using YCSB benchmarks, finding that DocumentDB delivered 20–33% higher read throughput, while FerretDB had lower tail latency for updates in mixed workloads, but noting the results are not conclusive. An open GitHub issue reports higher query latency in DocumentDB 1.0 than MongoDB 9.0.4 across several workloads, but the results have not been independently verified.

The DocumentDB release notes include upgrade paths and known issues. The project plans separate long-term support and development tracks, with its versioning policy still under discussion.

#9812. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

#9811. Crypto: Balancing Potential and Limitations – What Problems Can Digital Currencies Actually Solve?

The most enthusiastic crypto supporters once claimed (and some still do) that digital currencies can address all the flaws, risks, gaps, and shortcomings that burden the traditional financial system and that so many people are dissatisfied with. Except the reality has demonstrated they quite obviously can’t.

Crypto is indeed an exciting and promising innovation that has already proven it can be useful in many real-life situations, but that doesn’t automatically turn it into a fix-it-all. It’s not able to substitute fiat, nor can it single-handedly address issues like economic inequalities, structural inflation, security risks, and other similar problems.

However, if crypto were completely useless, we wouldn’t still be talking or hearing about it so often – but we are. If you want to know how far digital currencies have come and what’s happening in the crypto space at the moment, you can check out the Top Cryptocurrency News Today | Binance Square and read about the latest events and developments in the industry.

So, if crypto can’t bring world peace, what exactly can it do, and how far do its powers extend?

People were initially reluctant to engage with crypto and didn’t know what to make of it, but once the fear of the unknown subsided and curiosity took over, they realized that digital currencies possess certain qualities that can make them useful in various circumstances, as follows.

Diversification is a must in investment in order to reduce the risk of losses, and it relies on a simple principle of spreading capital across various types of assets with different risk profiles instead of concentrating it in a single one. Over the years, crypto has grown into quite a popular investment tool, even though it was intended to serve as a payment solution. Long story short, digital currencies have found their way into many investors’ holdings, and some of them have earned substantial profits from their crypto investments.

A portfolio can be well-balanced even if it doesn’t contain a single crypto, so digital assets aren’t a requirement for diversification. But the fact that they have a relatively low correlation to traditional markets, being driven by a different combination of factors, and can bring in outsized gains due to their sharp price swings makes them a good choice in this respect. Nevertheless, experts recommend keeping crypto allocations low (between 1% and 5% of a total portfolio) to protect against volatility risks.

Crypto is powered by blockchain technology, which means issuance and transactions are managed by a network of nodes instead of a single central entity, like governments, banks, and payment processors. This unique structure gives crypto the possibility to help with economic mobility.

By removing the intermediaries, coins can be transferred directly from one person to another, so the funds can arrive in the recipient’s wallet almost instantly, whereas with fiat, it can take up to several days for transactions to be processed, especially for international transfers that involve more cumbersome bureaucratic procedures.

Transaction speed is not the only aspect that crypto can improve, but affordability as well. Because there are no middlemen to incur processing fees, transferring crypto is cheaper than transferring conventional currencies.

And let’s not forget about all the people in the world who can’t use banking services because of all the barriers they impose. Crypto is easily accessible to everyone as long as they have a smart device and internet connection.

Another advantage that derives from crypto’s decentralized architecture is the ability to conceal users’ real identity. Crypto wallets are pseudonymous, so holders are not required to share sensitive data like legal names and personal addresses in order to use crypto. The blockchain also offers a public record of all the transactions it has ever processed, giving everyone the possibility to verify transfers and offering a level of transparency that fiat money cannot match.

The advantages that crypto offers seem absolutely amazing, but volatility casts a shadow over all these perks. Digital currencies can be a good addition to investors’ holdings, as they can offer high growth, but if the allocations are not well balanced, a market downturn can drag the entire portfolio down.

At the same time, the alleged decentralization that removes intermediaries from the equation and makes crypto transactions faster and cheaper in theory doesn’t always apply in practice. In many situations, crypto transactions run through centralized exchanges, or the projects are controlled by a foundation or corporate entity, which goes against the decentralization ethos that digital assets promote. So, instead of offering a different path to transferring value than traditional finance, crypto often uses the same centralized mechanism.

Using crypto to pay for goods and services is not practical because, once again, volatility gets in the way. With crypto values shifting constantly, it’s extremely challenging for companies that accept crypto payments to price their products and protect their profits. Many resort to payment processors to help them deal with volatility, but that kind of contradicts the whole idea of embracing crypto to bypass the middlemen.

It’s bold, if not downright absurd, to say that crypto can provide the answer to all of society’s money-related problems. But it’s equally absurd to dismiss it as a useless tool when it’s already being used in so many areas, and its integration into global finance continues to grow. Digital currencies can step in instances and areas where conventional banking services are either absent or highly inefficient. The takeaway here is that they can only serve as a complementary solution, not a complete replacement for traditional financial systems.

Financial Advice Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Cryptocurrency investments carry significant risks, and readers should conduct their own research before making financial decisions.
